docs.title: The engine for autonomous software production
docs.text:
zeroshot is an open-source workflow engine for coding agents. Write your team's development and QA process as a graph of implementation, independent review, testing, repair and delivery. Agents do the work; the graph decides what happens next, and the engine enforces its transitions and retry limits.

More examples on zeroshot.sh

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
1. Install the CLI:

    npm install --global @the-open-engine-company/zeroshot

  2. Run a first task with the built-in software-change graph.

  3. Build a review loop: write your own graph and runtime plan.

Working in ChatGPT, Codex or Claude? The plugin runs zeroshot without the CLI. Prefer a browser? zeroshot ui edits profiles, follows live runs and replays finished ones.

docs.title: What a run needs
docs.text:
• A graph: the steps, the routes between them and the typed state they share.
  • A runtime plan: the agent CLI, provider and model for each step, and the connections it needs.
  • An input: the task. zeroshot checks it against the graph before any agent starts.

Model output cannot add an edge or raise a bound. zeroshot records every step's result as the run advances, and closing the terminal does not stop the run. How execution works

docs.title: Built-in graphs
docs.text:
Run them as they are, or export one as the start of your own.

Graph What it does software-change Implements the task, runs acceptance and code review in parallel, repairs what they reject, then delivers. single-worker One agent, no review loop. pr-review Reviews a pull request. code-review Reviews a pull request in depth. auto-research Runs ten rounds of experiments by default. A new result replaces the current one only when the progress judge accepts it.

docs.title: Where it runs
docs.text: Target Where code and run state live Local Any folder on your machine (--cwd FOLDER). Git is optional without delivery. Install Self-hosted target Infrastructure you control. The target image checks out the source; agents and the run ledger stay there. Targets zeroshot Platform A managed target that takes the same graph and runtime plan, with accounts, organization policy and queues. Platform docs

docs.title: Where code is processed
docs.text: The target and the model provider are separate choices. Wherever a run happens, the agent sends its model provider the code and context it needs, so self-hosting zeroshot does not make model processing local. Check the provider's data-handling terms before running on client code. Runtimes and connections covers providers and credentials; for Platform, see the privacy notice and retention.

docs.title: zeroshot
docs.text:
Enforce your team's QA process on coding agents: run the graph you define locally or on named Zeroshot targets.

Single-result commands write JSON. Foreground `run`, `watch`, `logs`, and `attach` stream newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON).

Usage: zeroshot [COMMAND]

Commands:
  memory             Initialize local Active Memory through the canonical skill
  acp                Serve one local Zeroshot profile as an experimental ACP agent over stdio
  ui                 Serve the local profile editor and live or recorded run history
  target             Manage named targets or serve a direct target
  delegation         Manage user or organization machine delegations and API keys
  connection         Inspect and manage named runtime connections
  profile            Manage reusable graph/runtime profiles
  template           Inspect built-in graph templates
  stack              Validate, submit, and observe hosted stacks of dependent runs
  run                Submit a graph run locally or to a named target
  update             Update this executable and managed agent skills to the newest canonical release
  list               List runs as JSON
  status             Read a run's current status as JSON, including separate native delivery evidence when available
  watch              Follow durable status as NDJSON, including native delivery evidence independently of graph output
  logs               Follow a run's log stream as NDJSON
  attach             Attach to an execution's interactive event stream as NDJSON
  force-stop         Force a run to stop and write the result as JSON
  resume             Start a new attempt from a failed run's retained workspace or a saved checkpoint
  checkpoints        List one page of a run's saved workspace checkpoints as JSON
  export-workspace   Download a retained workspace or selected checkpoint as a tar archive
  discard-workspace  Permanently delete an abandoned retained target workspace
  version            Print the Zeroshot version
  help               Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -V, --version
          Print the Zeroshot version

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

docs.title: zeroshot memory init
docs.text:
Initialize local Active Memory or resume its saved work.

Creates a private session directory on the first call. Later calls return pending agent tasks, validate their responses, and publish after complete maintenance. The zeroshot-memory-init skill orchestrates the specialists using the host's connections. This command makes no model calls. It discovers all finished local runs and uses their recorded checkouts for current-source maintenance.

Usage: zeroshot memory init [OPTIONS] --directory <DIR>

Options:
      --ignore-repos <REPO>...
          Repositories to exclude by inventory alias: name, owner/repo, absolute path or repo ID. Comma-separated or repeated; saved with the session. Matching is exact and case-sensitive

      --ignore-graphs <GRAPH>...
          Graphs to exclude by exact authored root name or graph hash shown in the inventory. Comma-separated or repeated; saved with the session. Matching is exact and case-sensitive

      --directory <DIR>
          Private session directory outside repository checkouts; created if it does not exist

docs.title: zeroshot delegation
docs.text:
Manage user or organization machine delegations and API keys.

Requires human login. Set ZEROSHOT_API_KEY for unattended target commands; set ZEROSHOT_ORGANIZATION to select an organization with a user-owned key.

Usage: zeroshot delegation <COMMAND>

Commands:
  list     List delegation metadata without secret keys
  create   Create a delegation and its first API key. Prints the key once
  show     Read one delegation and its key metadata
  disable  Disable a delegation and revoke its access
  key      Create, inspect, or revoke a delegation's API keys
  help     Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

API keys act with their owner's current permissions and support every target command except delegation management. User-owned delegations follow the user's memberships; organization-owned delegations stay in one organization and require an owner or admin to manage. Keys expire after 90 days by default, with a maximum of 365 days. Creation prints the secret once. Store it in your CI secret store; do not put it in profiles, connections, or run input.

docs.title: zeroshot connection
docs.text:
Inspect and manage named runtime connections

Usage: zeroshot connection <COMMAND>

Commands:
  list    List connection metadata without secret values
  set     Create or replace one static connection
  delete  Delete one connection
  help    Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

CONNECTIONS
A runtime declares a connection key and the exact environment fields it needs. Zeroshot injects
only those fields; secret values never belong in runtime configuration.

`list` returns each key, scope, kind, and field names, never secret values. `set` creates or replaces
a complete static connection, so include every required field. Omit --target for local storage; use
--target NAME for hosted storage. Organization scope requires a hosted target.

Target-managed dynamic kinds are configured through the target rather than `connection set`; `list`
reports each connection's kind.

When a run reports `connection_unavailable`, list connections for the same target and scope, then
set the named key with every required field.

EXAMPLES
  zeroshot connection list
  zeroshot connection list --target prod --scope org
  zeroshot connection set openrouter --field OPENROUTER_API_KEY
  zeroshot connection set openrouter --target prod --field OPENROUTER_API_KEY

docs.title: zeroshot stack
docs.text:
Validate, submit, and observe hosted stacks of dependent runs

Usage: zeroshot stack <COMMAND>

Commands:
  validate    Validate a stack manifest without contacting a target
  submit      Atomically submit every node in a stack manifest
  status      Read a stack's aggregate status as JSON
  watch       Poll a stack and stream changed snapshots as NDJSON
  force-stop  Force every nonterminal run in a stack to stop
  help        Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

MANIFEST
The JSON manifest is strict and self-contained:

  {
    "schema": "zeroshot.stack/v1",
    "title": "Release checkout update",
    "delivery": "merge",
    "source": {"repository": "owner/repo", "branch": "main"},
    "profile": "org:software-change",
    "expiresAt": "<RFC3339 timestamp within 7 days>",
    "runs": {
      "backend": {"input": {"task": "Update the API."}},
      "integrate": {"needs": ["backend"], "input": {"task": "Run release tests."}}
    }
  }

Every run uses the same source and profile. Agent bindings must not declare `GH_TOKEN`; only the Git
delivery binding may declare it. `needs` gates readiness but does not pass output between runs.

DELIVERY
`delivery` is required and selects how every run lands:

  merge                  Each run merges into the base branch before the runs that need it start.
                         The profile must contain exactly one Git merge delivery node (merge@2 or
                         merge@3). A run may need several runs.
  stacked_pull_requests  Each run opens a pull request against the branch of the run before it, so
                         the stack arrives as a chain of pull requests and nothing is merged. The
                         profile must contain exactly one pull-request delivery node (pr@2).
                         Validation and submission turn the runs into one linear stack: each run
                         needs only the run before it, in dependency order with ties broken by run
                         name. `zeroshot stack validate` prints that order.

Platform assigns every run ID atomically at submission. After a node's dependencies succeed, Platform
materializes it against an exact source branch and revision, reported as `sourceBranch` and
`sourceRevision`. Once materialization completes, `readyAt` is set and the node's queue deadline is
the earlier of `expiresAt` and seven days after `readyAt`. `expiresAt` must be in the future and no
more than seven days away. Stacks cannot be edited or retried in place.

docs.title: zeroshot run
docs.text:
Submit a graph run locally or to a named target.

Local runs use --cwd or the invoking folder; Git worktrees use their root. Local Git delivery requires an attached, committed branch and an HTTPS/SSH remote. PR/merge also require a supported forge. Named targets require a committed Git source. Local workspaces must not overlap Zeroshot state. For local PR and merge delivery, the target is the branch's upstream when configured, otherwise the local branch name. Preparation verifies that the remote contains the target before agents start. To target `main` from a fresh worktree, run `git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/main`, or create the worktree from `origin/main`.

A foreground run follows NDJSON events until completion. --detach returns after submission. Ctrl-C before the submission attempt begins cancels the command; once it begins, Ctrl-C waits for the receipt and then detaches. During observation, Ctrl-C detaches without stopping the run.

Usage: zeroshot run [OPTIONS] --title <TITLE>

Options:
      --title <TITLE>
          Human-readable title recorded with the run

      --graph <FILE>
          Load a custom graph specification from this JSON file

      --template <TEMPLATE>
          Materialize and run this built-in graph template

          Possible values:
          - single-worker:   A single general-purpose worker
          - software-change: A review, validation, and optional delivery workflow for code changes
          - auto-research:   Research with ten iterations by default and independent evidence gates
          - issue-review:    Inspect an issue proposal and post a review report
          - pr-review:       Review a PR diff, conditionally reproduce behavior, and post a concise report
          - code-review:     Review a PR with parallel specialist reviewers, verify their findings, and post one report

      --input <FILE>
          Load the graph's initial input from this JSON file

      --task-from <URL>
          Resolve a GitHub issue or pull-request URL into review input before starting

      --runtime-config <FILE>
          Load an exact secret-free runtime plan from this JSON file

      --uniform-runtime-config <FILE>
          Expand one secret-free agent runtime across every executable graph node

      --environment <FILE>
          Load a JSON environment definition: setup, startup, public variables, and hook connections

      --no-environment
          Send an empty environment ({}) to bypass the target's configured default

      --profile <[SCOPE:]NAME>
          Use a profile: NAME, local:NAME, user:NAME, or org:NAME.

          When no profile or inline graph/runtime is supplied, scoped defaults are checked.

      --target <NAME>
          Run on this named target; if omitted, run locally

      --cwd <FOLDER>
          Working folder (default: invoking folder). File arguments stay relative to the invoking folder

      --source-connection <KEY>
          Named connection for Git checkout and push.

          HTTPS uses GIT_USERNAME and GIT_PASSWORD; SSH uses GIT_SSH_PRIVATE_KEY and GIT_SSH_KNOWN_HOSTS.

      --source-provider <PROVIDER>
          Forge provider ID for the selected Git remote (for example source.github or source.gitlab)

      --source-base-url <URL>
          Public HTTPS base URL of the forge instance, including any installation path

      --repository <REPOSITORY>
          Repository in GitHub owner/name form or a credential-free HTTPS/SSH Git URL. Requires --target

      --branch <BRANCH>
          Source branch to resolve for the named run. Requires --target

      --revision <SHA>
          Exact source commit SHA. Requires --target

      --submission-key <KEY>
          Stable idempotency key for safely retrying submission

  -d, --detach
          Return after submission instead of following NDJSON run events

      --validate-only
          Validate and materialize the run without submitting it or running preparation scripts.

          Remote profiles still require target access. This does not check dependency installation or connection availability.

      --forward-gh-token
          Send the GH_TOKEN from this shell with the submission.

          Without this flag the target uses its own stored GitHub connection, and a GH_TOKEN in this shell is not sent. Fails when GH_TOKEN is unset.

      --delivery <MODE>
          Template delivery mode. Defaults to pull_request for software-change, comment for issue-review, pr-review and code-review, otherwise none

      --push
          Commit and push the managed run branch without opening a pull request

      --pr
          Materialize pull-request delivery for the software-change template

      --ship
          Materialize merge delivery for the software-change template

      --no-pr-feedback
          Do not route visible pull-request feedback through the autonomous repair loop

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

RUNTIME CONFIGURATION
    The file is secret-free JSON. For example:

      {
        "harness": "codex",
        "provider": "openrouter",
        "size": "medium",
        "nodes": {
          "worker": {
            "kind": "agent",
            "model": "provider-model-id",
            "connections": {"openrouter": ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"]}
          }
        }
      }

    The host's adapter registry admits supported harness/provider pairs. See the Harness adapters
    documentation for available pairs. Official local builds include contributed opencode and hermes.
    Contributed adapters use the same feature contract; compatibility is community-maintained.
    Platform and the default target image enable only core harnesses. Gateway connections
    require GATEWAY_BASE_URL and GATEWAY_API_KEY. Codex uses Responses and Claude uses Messages.
    Pi, Copilot, OpenCode, and Hermes gateway lanes also carry GATEWAY_API, which names the protocol as
    openai-responses, openai-completions, or anthropic-messages.
    Declaring ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL with ANTHROPIC_API_KEY sends the pi/anthropic lane to a
    caller-owned Anthropic Messages endpoint.
    The codex/foundry and claude/foundry lanes require AZURE_FOUNDRY_API_KEY with either
    AZURE_FOUNDRY_RESOURCE or AZURE_FOUNDRY_BASE_URL; the model is the Foundry deployment name.
    Known-incompatible harness/provider pairs include
    codex/anthropic and claude/openai. Local copilot/github reuses native login; contained
    copilot/github uses a user-backed GitHub connection with COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN.
    Copilot's other lanes use native BYOK transports; its Bedrock lane uses AWS's Responses API. Pi has no permission
    control of its own, so its contained runs rely on the disposable capsule rather than a bypass
    argument. Model IDs are passed
    unchanged to the selected harness and
    provider; Zeroshot does not maintain or validate provider model catalogs.

    Size identifiers are target-owned strings. List offered sizes with `zeroshot target sizes NAME`.
    Omit size to use the target default; the target decides whether a requested size is available.

    Every executable graph node needs a same-named binding. Agent bindings require kind and model.
    Optional fields are effort (low, medium, high, xhigh, or max when supported), sessionScope
    (execution or node_instance), and connections. Each connection key maps to the exact
    environment variable names required by that node; never put values in this file.

    The run-level harness and provider are the default lane. An agent binding may add
    "lane": {"harness": "claude", "provider": "anthropic"} to run that node on another accepted
    pair; git_delivery and comment_delivery bindings cannot. --uniform-runtime-config applies one lane to every agent
    node. Named targets must advertise per-node lane support (openengine.node-runtime-lanes/v1), and
    targets advertise enabled pairs through openengine.runtime-harnesses/v1. A local run first checks
    that each registered lane's executable is on PATH.

    Use `zeroshot template show TEMPLATE` to inspect node names. With --push, --pr, or --ship, omit the
    template-owned delivery binding.

    --uniform-runtime-config requires harness, provider, and model. It accepts optional size,
    effort, sessionScope, connections, activeMemory, and globalAgents fields without nodes.
    Zeroshot expands that agent binding
    across every executable graph node and supplies graph-visible Git delivery bindings itself.
    Omitted connections reuse native local authentication when the selected adapter supports it;
    other local lanes and contained targets derive their canonical connection requirements.

ENVIRONMENT PREPARATION
    For Docker or Platform targets, pass --environment environment.json with a separate, flat JSON
    definition (not a profile field or an "environment" wrapper):

      {
        "setup": "apt-get update && apt-get install -y jq",
        "startup": "npm ci",
        "variables": {"CI": "true"}
      }

    Setup runs as root before checkout or workspace restore. Startup runs as the non-root
    workspace owner in the checkout before any agent starts. Workers and reviewers share the
    prepared workspace. Both hooks rerun on resume; startup must tolerate existing files.

    Install OS packages in setup, project dependencies in startup, and shared executable tools
    under $ZEROSHOT_TOOLS/bin (already on every hook and agent's PATH). Shell exports last only
    for that hook; use variables for public values shared with agents. Scripts and variables
    are public. If hooks need secrets, add e.g. "connections": {"package-registry": ["NPM_TOKEN"]}.
    Hook connections are separate from node connections.

    Hook failures stop the run before agents start and use no graph retry attempts.
    Inspect `zeroshot logs RUN_ID --target NAME` for preparation output.
    Omit both flags to allow host defaults; direct Docker defaults to the base environment.
    --no-environment sends {} to bypass host defaults. Local runs use the invoking machine and
    reject hooks and hook connections.

    Installation, services, limits, and recovery:
    https://the-open-engine.github.io/zeroshot/current/guides/runtime-environments/

EXIT STATUS
    0  The run succeeded, --detach or Ctrl-C returned before it finished, or --validate-only
       accepted it.
    1  The run finished failed, or the command failed. A failed run's summary is printed on
       stderr. `zeroshot watch RUN_ID` waits for a detached run and exits the same way.

docs.title: zeroshot distribution contract
docs.text: .github/workflows/release.yml is the only zeroshot release workflow. An operator supplies an X.Y.Z version with an exact commit on main; the workflow rejects versions before major 8.

docs.title: Canonical identity
docs.text:
Release item Identity Git tag and release vX.Y.Z Executables zeroshot and restic (.exe on Windows) Native archives zeroshot-vX.Y.Z-<target>.tar.gz Target manifest distribution/zeroshot-targets.json npm package @the-open-engine-company/zeroshot Run skill npm skills/zeroshot/SKILL.md; release asset zeroshot-skill.md Memory init skill npm skills/zeroshot-memory-init/SKILL.md; release asset zeroshot-memory-init-skill.md Graph design skill npm skills/zeroshot-graph-design/SKILL.md; release asset zeroshot-graph-design-skill.md Plan skill npm skills/zeroshot-plan/SKILL.md; release asset zeroshot-plan-skill.md Target image ghcr.io/the-open-engine/zeroshot-target Python wheel release zeroshot-python-vX.Y.Z_1 Python package the-open-engine-zeroshot==X.Y.Z.post1 when PyPI publication is enabled Minor documentation vX.Y/ at its newest patch, including Python SDK revision 1

The workflow publishes no alternate tag prefix, package, image, executable alias, source-build fallback, or compatibility artifact.

The npm installer copies every managed skill to $HOME/.agents/skills/<skill-name> for Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Pi, and to ${CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR:-$HOME/.claude}/skills/<skill-name> for Claude Code. Each skill has one canonical source across hosts. These fixed user scopes are installed by default so agents added later need no zeroshot reinstall. Package updates and zeroshot update replace only an unchanged managed copy. An edited or conflicting skill is preserved and fails installation visibly. npm 7 and newer provide no uninstall lifecycle, so users remove unchanged managed copies from these documented paths when they uninstall the package.

Set ZEROSHOT_SKIP_SKILLS=1 to skip skill installation during npm install and zeroshot update. Executables still install or update, and existing skills stay untouched.

Older updaters install only the skills they know. If zeroshot-graph-design or zeroshot-plan is missing after an executable upgrade, run zeroshot update again. The current updater installs or refreshes every managed skill even when the executable version is already current.

docs.title: Targets
docs.text:
The target manifest declares Linux x64/arm64 musl, macOS x64/arm64, and Windows x64, and the npm target table must match it exactly. The installer stops on any other host.

Every archive contains exactly the zeroshot executable and its pinned Restic sidecar. npm, Python wheels, self-update, and the target image install the pair together. The 10.4.0 through 10.8.0 updaters predate the sidecar and reject these archives, so those installations upgrade once through npm as described in Install zeroshot. SHA256SUMS covers each archive and the exact zeroshot-skill.md, zeroshot-memory-init-skill.md, zeroshot-graph-design-skill.md, and zeroshot-plan-skill.md copied from their canonical npm sources. The workflow also rejects a Linux zeroshot release binary that has a dynamic interpreter.

The exact archive layout is an updater compatibility contract. Adding an archive entry strands every released updater: each rejects unknown entries before it can install a newer executable. Changing the extractor in a new release cannot repair those installed updaters; users must reinstall through npm to cross that boundary. Keep additional release assets outside the native archives.

docs.title: Version staging
docs.text: Checked-in manifests carry development versions that are not release identifiers. In the release workspace, scripts/distribution.js stage-version updates zeroshot/Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock, then check-version verifies their coupling before compilation. Release automation does not commit those staged versions.

docs.title: Publication order
docs.text:
Step Release action 1 Build and smoke all native archives. 2 Generate and verify SHA256SUMS. 3 Build and smoke docker/zeroshot-target/Dockerfile from the same commit. 4 Create or verify the canonical GitHub Release and its exact assets. 5 Publish the image version, source-commit, and eligible latest tags. 6 Pack, install, smoke, and publish @the-open-engine-company/zeroshot. 7 Build and publish Python SDK revision 1 as an immutable GitHub wheel release. 8 Publish that wheel set to PyPI; use publish_pypi: false only when trusted publishing is unavailable. 9 Publish into vX.Y/; update the legacy stable redirect for the newest release.

The canonical release dispatches release-python.yml on main as a standalone workflow with the exact release source, version, revision 1, and publish_pypi selection. It records the returned run ID and waits for success before publishing documentation. This keeps PyPI OIDC in its configured standalone publisher; reusable workflow publication is unsupported.

PUBLISHING.md contains the operator setup and recovery rules.

docs.title: Caller-owned delivery validation
docs.text:
Local callers may select ZEROSHOT_DELIVERY_CHECK_COMMAND as one absolute private executable outside of the checkout. Its path crosses the private controller bootstrap, never graph input or provider environments. This is a trusted local integration point, not an OS isolation boundary against the same user. Hosted profiles cannot select a local executable.

Before pushing the captured candidate (publish), immediately after a PR is synchronized (published), while observing an open review (review), and immediately before requesting a merge (merge), delivery sends openengine.delivery-validation/v1 JSON on stdin. It includes the publication stage, repository, branches, exact head and tree, trusted review base when available, and verifier-authored title and body. No delivery credential is supplied. The helper returns exactly one verdict: accepted, pending, repair with a public-safe reason, or refused with a public-safe reason. Pending keeps polling; repair enters the authored repair/review loop; refusal, malformed output and process failure stop the execution. Pending observation does not hide CI or new feedback; pending publication and merge block those effects. Acceptance cannot override forge policy, required checks, reviews or merge queues.

The helper has no imposed turn deadline. Bounded pipes and cancellation use the normal process session; its process tree must be confirmed gone before delivery releases the workspace, even if the outer operation is cancelled. An accepted helper must leave the captured candidate clean and unchanged. Forge confirmation remains authoritative: accepting or queuing a merge is not a merged receipt.

The published-stage notification precedes the first policy/status read, so a caller can durably record the actual PR even when a subsequent inspection fails. Terminal merged/closed observations settle before review-stage hooks or late feedback. A completed remote merge cannot become another repair.

docs.title: How execution works
docs.text:
Your graph decides what runs next. After each step, zeroshot validates the result, updates the shared state and follows the graph's rules. Agents cannot add steps or increase retry limits.

For example, a graph can send a worker's change to two reviewers, return rejected work for repair and stop after four attempts. The reviewers judge the change; zeroshot enforces the route and limit. Build a review loop implements that example.

docs.title: Before a run starts
docs.text:
A run needs four inputs:

Input Purpose Title Identifies the run in lists and status output Graph Defines steps, shared state, routes, limits and results Initial input Supplies the task in the format the graph expects Runtime plan Chooses each agent's harness, provider, model and connections

Before starting a local controller or submitting to a target, zeroshot checks the graph, runtime bindings and input. For a target-stored profile, it fetches the profile first and applies the same checks. --validate-only runs these checks without starting a run.

docs.title: Graph nodes
docs.text:
step and verifier nodes do the work. Groups control their execution:

Group Behavior seq Runs children in order choice Selects a branch from the declared signals par Runs branches concurrently and joins their results loop Repeats a body within a fixed limit map Runs a bounded body for array items succeed and fail End the graph

Routes and conditions are structured data, not executable code or prompt instructions. The graph contract defines their fields.

docs.title: How results choose the next step
docs.text:
Each agent returns a value through its declared output channel. zeroshot validates that value, updates state using the graph's bindings, then evaluates what runs next.

In a repair loop, a reviewer returns a decision and feedback. The graph routes an acceptance onward or a rejection back for repair. maxIterations still applies if an agent asks to continue.

docs.title: Working in parallel
docs.text:
Parallel agents share a workspace. Coordinate writers so they do not overwrite each other's changes, and place reviewers after the writers when they need the finished result. Reviewers see the same dependencies, generated files and services as workers.

Put Git delivery after all writing and review branches have joined. Graph validation rejects concurrent delivery alongside another executable node, or inside a map that can have multiple items.

docs.title: Run history and cleanup
docs.text:
Each run has an ID and a SQLite ledger. Closing the terminal, disconnecting a client or cancelling a Python await does not stop the controller. Reconnect to inspect the run or stop it explicitly; see Observe and control runs.

The controller cleans up execution activity when the run ends. Cleanup guarantees differ by OS; process cleanup describes detached child processes.

docs.title: Built-in templates are ordinary graphs
docs.text:
Use a built-in graph as it is, or export it to make your own:

zeroshot template list
zeroshot template show software-change

template show prints a tree, marking executable nodes with *. Add --json or redirect stdout to export the complete GraphSpec.

Template Purpose software-change Implement, review, repair and deliver a change single-worker Run one agent without a review loop pr-review Review a PR and post a concise comment code-review Review a PR in depth and post verified findings issue-review Review an issue proposal auto-research Run experiments and retain results accepted by a reviewer

software-change opens a PR by default. Choose delivery with:

Option Result --delivery none Keep the accepted change local --push Push the run branch without opening a PR --pr Open or update a PR, address feedback and wait for CI; leave merging to you --ship Follow the same review loop, then merge under the repository's policy

Required approval blocks --ship, but not --pr. For local PR and merge runs, the target branch is the current branch's upstream, or its local name when no upstream is set. See source and delivery setup.

PR feedback is enabled by default and restricted to repository writers. --no-pr-feedback disables it; feedback rules cover permission checks.

auto-research runs ten rounds by default; options.iterations changes the count. Results stay in .zeroshot/research; --push publishes each accepted round. See research rounds and repair for the full behavior.

docs.title: Runtimes and connections
docs.text:
A graph defines the work and its control flow; the runtime plan supplies execution details for each executable node. Since the two documents are separate, local, self-hosted, and managed targets can run the same graph.

The RuntimePlan reference lists every field, limit, and admission rule.

docs.title: Four explicit choices
docs.text:
Each agent node uses:

  1. a harness enabled by the host;
  2. a provider supported by that harness;
  3. an opaque provider-owned model identifier;
  4. zero or more named connections, each declaring exact environment field names.

The harness and provider form the node's effective lane. A plan's run-level harness and provider are the default lane for every agent node, and a binding can override them with its own lane, for example to have Codex implement and Claude Code review. zeroshot starts one harness adapter per distinct effective lane, and each node runs on its own lane's CLI. Model and connections are always chosen per node.

Harness adapters lists available adapters and accepted harness/provider pairs, which apply to the default lane and to every node's lane. Admission rejects known-incompatible pairs, such as codex with anthropic and claude with openai. zeroshot does not check current provider availability, and model names remain provider-owned.

docs.title: Uniform and exact plans
docs.text:
--uniform-runtime-config expands one agent binding across all executable nodes, which keeps a built-in template configuration short:

{
  "harness": "claude",
  "provider": "anthropic",
  "model": "PROVIDER_MODEL_ID",
  "size": "medium",
  "effort": "high",
  "sessionScope": "execution"
}

--runtime-config accepts a full plan with one same-named binding per executable graph node. Use it when reviewers and workers need different lanes, models, effort, sessions, or connections. Inspect node names first with zeroshot template show TEMPLATE.

Session scope decides whether a node that runs again, such as in a loop, continues its provider session; see session scope.

docs.title: Runtime configuration contains names, not secret values
docs.text:
A connection maps a stable key to required environment field names:

{
  "connections": {
    "openrouter": ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"]
  }
}

The submission environment or a target-owned connection store supplies the values. zeroshot keeps them out of the graph, runtime JSON, run ledger, and observation records.

When connections is omitted, zeroshot materializes provider access for each node from its effective lane and the selected execution placement. Local adapters can reuse native authentication as described in Harness adapters. Lanes requiring a connection and contained targets receive these canonical requirements:

Provider Connection key Fields openai openai OPENAI_API_KEY openrouter openrouter OPENROUTER_API_KEY anthropic anthropic ANTHROPIC_API_KEY gateway gateway GATEWAY_BASE_URL, GATEWAY_API_KEY bedrock bedrock AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK, AWS_REGION foundry foundry AZURE_FOUNDRY_API_KEY, AZURE_FOUNDRY_RESOURCE github github COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN opencode, opencode-go opencode OPENCODE_API_KEY

Pi, Copilot, OpenCode and Hermes gateway runs additionally require GATEWAY_API, which names the wire protocol (openai-responses, openai-completions, or anthropic-messages). The Codex and Claude gateway lanes do not use it.

A run's connection requirements are the union over its nodes. A contained run with a Codex/OpenAI worker and Claude/Anthropic reviewers can therefore require both OPENAI_API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.

Compatible authored connections take precedence, including CODEX_API_KEY for contained OpenAI access and Claude's supported auth-token variables for contained Anthropic access. Local profiles keep the authored runtime unchanged; applying one to a target derives the contained requirements at submission time. Profiles stored on a target derive those requirements when they are stored.

Local Claude workers and reviewers preserve the invoking shell's USER for macOS Keychain login and reuse native CLAUDE.md, plugins, and MCP configuration. Claude's --safe-mode applies only to the permission-settings probe before a model turn. Hosted runs use private homes and do not inherit the caller's USER or user configuration. Declare additional environment fields needed by MCP servers through runtime connections.

Store a local static connection by prompting for its fields:

zeroshot connection set openrouter --field OPENROUTER_API_KEY
zeroshot connection list

connection set replaces the whole value for that key, so repeat every required --field when updating a multi-field connection. connection list reports names and kind but never values.

Hosted targets can also own user- or organization-scoped connections. Setup and dynamic connection kinds depend on the target; zeroshot consumes only the resolved fields declared by the runtime.

Source delivery selects its own credentials independently of agent model providers. GitHub uses GH_TOKEN; GitLab uses GITLAB_TOKEN. Local delivery can reuse the selected host's native gh or glab login. See forge delivery setup for explicit instances, Git transport credentials, and target connection examples.

docs.title: Gateways
docs.text:
To use a gateway, set provider: "gateway" and use the gateway's model identifier:

{ "harness": "codex", "provider": "gateway", "model": "PROVIDER_MODEL_ID" }

Store the endpoint and key together through the existing connection command:

zeroshot connection set gateway --field GATEWAY_BASE_URL --field GATEWAY_API_KEY

Codex requires the OpenAI Responses API, including streaming and tool calls; Chat Completions alone is insufficient. It sends the key as a bearer token. Claude requires the Anthropic Messages API and sends the key in x-api-key. The Pi, Copilot, OpenCode and Hermes gateway lanes let the caller name the wire protocol in GATEWAY_API and use the selected native transport without probing it; an unrecognized value fails before launch. The selected gateway/model must support the harness's requests, including structured output. zeroshot does not probe capabilities or translate protocols.

Supply the base URL expected by the selected harness, including any gateway path prefix. zeroshot preserves that path. For OpenRouter, use https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 with Codex or https://openrouter.ai/api with Claude. Base URLs must use HTTP(S) and cannot contain embedded credentials, query parameters, or fragments. Both fields remain connection values, outside runtime JSON and run history. Exact plans declare these fields under any chosen connection key.

docs.title: Microsoft Foundry
docs.text:
The codex and claude harnesses reach models deployed in a Microsoft Foundry resource with provider: "foundry". The model is the Foundry deployment name:

{ "harness": "claude", "provider": "foundry", "model": "FOUNDRY_DEPLOYMENT_NAME" }

Store the API key with the resource name:

zeroshot connection set foundry --field AZURE_FOUNDRY_API_KEY --field AZURE_FOUNDRY_RESOURCE

For a custom domain, declare AZURE_FOUNDRY_BASE_URL instead of AZURE_FOUNDRY_RESOURCE, set to the resource root without an API path. Exactly one of the two must be present. Claude Code runs in its native Foundry mode against https://RESOURCE.services.ai.azure.com/anthropic, or the root URL followed by /anthropic. Codex uses the Azure OpenAI v1 Responses API at https://RESOURCE.openai.azure.com/openai/v1, or the root URL followed by /openai/v1, and sends the key in the api-key header. One connection therefore serves a run that mixes Codex and Claude nodes on the same resource. Foundry lanes accept API keys only; Microsoft Entra ID authentication is not supported.

Docker runtimes can prepare shared tools, project dependencies, and services with setup and startup hooks. See Prepare a runtime environment for the installation conventions, resume behavior, and direct-target ownership boundary.

docs.title: Renewable local GitHub delivery credentials
docs.text:
A trusted local host can set ZEROSHOT_GITHUB_TOKEN_FILE to a private token file outside the checkout. Use a delivery binding with "connections": {}: the controller receives the credential without adding it to agent bindings. The file contains one token, optionally followed by a newline. It must be a regular file owned by the controller user with no access for other users.

The host obtains short-lived tokens and renews them by atomically replacing the file. Mount its parent directory if the host writes outside a container. zeroshot reopens the path on each delivery visit and after authentication rejection; an unchanged rejected token waits for host renewal. Explicit GH_TOKEN takes precedence, including failing on an empty or malformed value.

The file setting and credential stay out of provider environments, profiles, run history, and recovery metadata. Resume selects the caller's current setting again and retains the delivery branch identity. This keeps credentials out of agent environments; it does not isolate a trusted controller from other processes running as the same OS user. Named targets continue to use their existing credential resolver.

docs.title: Trusted local delivery validation
docs.text: Set ZEROSHOT_DELIVERY_CHECK_COMMAND to one absolute executable path outside the checkout to validate publication and merge candidates. It must be private to the controller user and executable; this setting accepts no command arguments or shell expression. The controller owns its process and passes candidate facts through the delivery validation protocol. The caller selects this capability outside graph and runtime input. The setting stays out of provider context and run/recovery history, and resume selects the caller's current executable again.

docs.title: Targets
docs.text:
A target is where your agents run and their run history is stored. Choose it independently of the graph and models.

Target Use it for Source Local Work in a folder on your machine Your existing files, including uncommitted changes Direct Docker Run on infrastructure you manage An exact committed Git revision Hosted Use a service such as zeroshot Platform An exact committed Git revision

The model provider still receives the code and context its agent needs. Self-hosting the target does not make model processing local.

docs.title: Run locally
docs.text:
Omit --target for a local run. Add --cwd FOLDER to choose the workspace; otherwise zeroshot uses the invoking folder. A folder inside a Git checkout resolves to its root. Input and configuration file paths remain relative to where you invoked the command.

Local agents edit this workspace as your user. With --delivery none, Git is optional. Install and sign in to every agent CLI your runtime plan uses. zeroshot checks for executables before starting; a missing login fails at the agent's first turn.

Keep the workspace separate from the active zeroshot state directory. Independent workspaces can run concurrently, but overlapping folders cannot. Set ZEROSHOT_STATE_DIR outside the workspace if needed.

Local Codex and Claude runs respect configured permission policies. When none is configured, zeroshot may add permission-bypass flags. Reviewers share the workspace; their instruction not to edit reviewed files is not filesystem isolation. See local authentication and permissions for each harness's behavior.

docs.title: Workspace snapshot disk usage
docs.text:
Snapshots include ignored files such as node_modules/ and target/. Where filesystem cloning is unavailable, staging needs another full workspace copy as well as checkpoint storage. Concurrent runs increase peak usage. Remove unnecessary build artifacts or keep large generated directories outside the workspace when disk space is tight.

Restic failures report the operation and failure stage or exit status without exposing private child output. A failed backup leaves the previous published checkpoint available.

docs.title: Run a Docker target
docs.text:
The Docker image includes zeroshot and its core agent CLIs. It is published for linux/amd64. Start a persistent target and register it with your CLI:

docker run --detach --restart unless-stopped --name zeroshot-target \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \
  -v zeroshot-data:/var/lib/zeroshot \
  ghcr.io/the-open-engine/zeroshot-target:latest

zeroshot target add local-target \
  --url http://127.0.0.1:8080 \
  --direct

Direct targets have no authentication

Keep the port on loopback or a trusted private network. Before broader exposure, add an authenticated reverse proxy that forwards WebSockets.

Add --target local-target to run and observation commands. Open http://127.0.0.1:8080/ui/ for profiles and run history. The zeroshot-data volume preserves both when the container is recreated. If you change the browser origin, set --public-origin to match it.

Docker must be running. The restart policy recovers from reboots and unexpected exits; after a manual stop, use docker start zeroshot-target. Interrupted runs are marked lost. If recovery data exists, start a successor with zeroshot resume RUN_ID --target local-target.

Docker and hosted runs use the remote Git revision, not your uncommitted files. --cwd chooses the client checkout used to select that source. Its upstream takes precedence; otherwise zeroshot selects the unique eligible HTTPS or SSH remote. For ambiguous remotes, set an upstream or pass --repository with a credential-free clone URL or GitHub owner/name. Use --branch and --revision to select a branch and exact commit. Detached worktrees need repository and branch overrides. Generic Git transport requires a target advertising openengine.git-transport/v1.

If a submission reply is lost, zeroshot retries with the same submission key. If it still cannot confirm the result, check zeroshot list --target NAME or rerun with the reported --submission-key KEY to recover the same run.

docs.title: Image tags and remote hosts
docs.text:
Pin ghcr.io/the-open-engine/zeroshot-target:X.Y.Z or an image digest for a stable deployment. latest advances with releases; sha-COMMIT tags identify their source.

For a remote machine, keep its port on loopback and open an SSH tunnel:

ssh -N -L 8080:127.0.0.1:8080 USER@HOST
zeroshot target add remote-target --url http://127.0.0.1:8080 --direct

Keep the tunnel open. If port 8080 is taken locally, forward another port and set the target's --public-origin to that origin, such as http://127.0.0.1:18080. The target image README covers proxies, Docker access and image builds.

docs.title: Use a hosted target
docs.text:
For zeroshot Platform, run zeroshot target login platform, then use --target platform. To register another hosting service:

zeroshot target add production --url https://TARGET_ORIGIN
zeroshot target login production

The service manages login, source access, organization connections, queues and capacity. See the Platform docs for its setup.

docs.title: API keys
docs.text:
For CI, sign in as a human and create a delegation:

zeroshot target login platform
zeroshot delegation create ci

Store the one-time api_key as ZEROSHOT_API_KEY in your CI secret store. It carries your current permissions. Keys expire after 90 days by default; --expires-in-days accepts 1–365. Set ZEROSHOT_ORGANIZATION to the organization UUID when a user key needs organization selection.

Organization owners and admins can create an organization delegation instead:

zeroshot delegation create release --owner org --organization ORGANIZATION_UUID

Organization keys stay in their organization. Omitted profile and connection scopes follow the owner's scope. Keep provider and source credentials in their usual connections.

Unset ZEROSHOT_API_KEY and use human login to manage delegations. Create a replacement key before revoking the old one:

zeroshot delegation list
zeroshot delegation key create DELEGATION_ID --name rotation
zeroshot delegation key revoke DELEGATION_ID OLD_KEY_ID
zeroshot delegation disable DELEGATION_ID

Revocation blocks further calls; already accepted runs continue.

docs.title: Workspace export protocol
docs.text: To download files, see Download a retained workspace. For hosting integrations, see the workspace export contract.

docs.title: Sizes and supported agents
docs.text:
Run zeroshot target sizes NAME to list available sizes; add --json for structured output. Omitting a size uses the target's default. Local execution and direct targets offer host, using the machine's resources. The target decides which other sizes are available.

Official local builds include contributed adapters; Platform and the default Docker image include core adapters only. Check harness support before choosing a runtime. Target discovery specifies size and adapter negotiation.

docs.title: Source and delivery credentials
docs.text:
Local Git operations can reuse your Git authentication. PR and merge delivery support GitHub and GitLab; other Git hosts support checkout and push. See forge setup.

For local PR and merge runs, the target branch is the current branch's upstream, or its local name when no upstream is set. To target main from a fresh worktree, run git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/main, or create the worktree from origin/main. zeroshot verifies that the remote contains the branch before starting agents.

Contained targets do not inherit your Git login. --source-connection KEY selects transport credentials: GIT_USERNAME and GIT_PASSWORD for HTTPS, or GIT_SSH_PRIVATE_KEY and GIT_SSH_KNOWN_HOSTS for SSH. These credentials are separate from agent model connections.

Named targets normally resolve GitHub access from their stored github connection. To forward local GH_TOKEN for GitHub.com checkout and delivery, pass --forward-gh-token to run, resume or stack submit. The flag fails if the token is unset and does not apply it to another Git host. It can also fill a declared GH_TOKEN connection field and support direct-target --task-from resolution. Model nodes receive credentials only through their declared connections.

Transport secrets stay out of source records, history and checkpoints. Direct-target resume keeps the original source authorization and resolves fresh values. The submission receipt reports the selected repository, branch and revision; uncommitted files stay on the client.

docs.title: Run a first task
docs.text: Run the built-in software-change graph on a project folder. One agent makes the change, acceptance and code review check it independently, and anything they reject goes back for repair. This run leaves the result in your folder instead of opening a pull request.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• zeroshot is installed.
  • One agent CLI is installed and signed in: Codex, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot or Pi. zeroshot uses its login. Check it with codex --version, claude --version, copilot --version or pi --version.
  • You are in the project folder. Git is optional; add --cwd FOLDER to the commands to work on another folder.

The agent edits this folder

Commit or back up anything you want to keep first.

docs.title: 1. Write the task
docs.text:
Save it as input.json. Replace the task with a small change that fits your project.

input.json
{
  "task": "Add JSON output to the status command and cover it with focused tests."
}

docs.title: 2. Pick the agent
docs.text:
Save the one for your CLI as runtime.json, and replace YOUR_MODEL_ID with a model your provider accepts. zeroshot passes it on unchanged.

CodexClaude CodeGitHub CopilotPi runtime.json
{
  "harness": "codex",
  "provider": "openai",
  "model": "YOUR_MODEL_ID",
  "effort": "high"
}
runtime.json
{
  "harness": "claude",
  "provider": "anthropic",
  "model": "YOUR_MODEL_ID",
  "effort": "high"
}
runtime.json
{
  "harness": "copilot",
  "provider": "github",
  "model": "YOUR_MODEL_ID"
}
runtime.json
{
  "harness": "pi",
  "provider": "anthropic",
  "model": "YOUR_MODEL_ID",
  "effort": "high"
}

A local run needs no API key. Docker and Platform runs cannot use your CLI's login; they need the provider's API key (OPENAI_API_KEY for Codex) from your environment or the target's connection store. Runtimes and connections explains both. Harness adapters lists every agent and provider pair.

docs.title: 3. Check it
docs.text:
--validate-only checks the input, graph and runtime without starting anything. Each command here is one line, so it pastes into Bash, PowerShell or Command Prompt.

zeroshot run --title "Add JSON status output" --template software-change --delivery none --input input.json --uniform-runtime-config runtime.json --validate-only

It prints {"valid":true}, or names the input, graph or runtime problem. Connections are checked later, when the target receives the run.

docs.title: 4. Run it
docs.text:
Drop --validate-only:

zeroshot run --title "Add JSON status output" --template software-change --delivery none --input input.json --uniform-runtime-config runtime.json

The command streams the run as JSON lines. Ctrl-C closes the stream, not the run. From another terminal:

zeroshot list
zeroshot status RUN_ID
zeroshot logs RUN_ID

To follow the graph and each agent's transcript, run zeroshot ui and open the run under Runs.

docs.title: When it ends
docs.text: A run ends when the graph reaches a terminal node, when you run zeroshot force-stop RUN_ID, or when the engine or target fails. A failed foreground run exits with status 1 and prints its latest error records, then the zeroshot logs command that shows the rest. Observe and control runs covers resuming a failed run.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Open a pull request instead. Replace --delivery none with --pr. This needs a clean Git checkout with a commit, a remote and forge access. Move input.json and runtime.json outside the checkout first, and update --input and --uniform-runtime-config to their new paths. Commit or stash any changes left by your first run, then check git status --short for remaining changes before starting the PR run.
  • See the graph you ran. zeroshot template show software-change --delivery none prints it as a tree. Names marked * need runtime bindings. Add --json to export the GraphSpec that --graph and the Python SDK accept.
  • Go smaller. zeroshot template show single-worker is one agent with no review loop.
  • Research instead of change. zeroshot template show auto-research runs ten iterations by default; set options.iterations in the input to change that. Results stay under .zeroshot/research; add --push to publish each finalized iteration.
  • Write your own graph. Build a review loop goes step by step.

docs.title: Install zeroshot
docs.text:
Install with Node.js 18 or newer:

npm install --global @the-open-engine-company/zeroshot

This installs the native CLI and its agent skills. Releases support Linux and macOS on x64 and arm64, and Windows on x64. Node.js is needed for installation; zeroshot itself is a Rust executable.

To use zeroshot through ChatGPT, Codex or Claude without the CLI, install the plugin.

docs.title: Prepare a local run
docs.text:
Install and sign in to the agent CLI you want to use: Codex, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot or Pi. Put it on PATH. Claude Code requires version 2.1.310 or newer; see harness adapters for all supported agents and providers.

Local runs can reuse supported native logins. Other providers and contained targets need connections. For example:

zeroshot connection set openai --field OPENAI_API_KEY

Choose a project folder. A local run with --delivery none edits that folder and needs no Git repository. Opening a PR also requires a clean checkout, a remote and forge access; GitHub delivery needs gh on PATH.

Run a first task walks through the input, agent configuration and run command.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text: Use PowerShell or Command Prompt. Install Git for Windows and put Git and your agent CLI on PATH; npm .cmd launchers work. If your Codex permissions require its native Windows sandbox, complete that setup too. zeroshot does not install it. See Windows paths for configuration and state locations.

docs.title: Open the workspace UI
docs.text:
zeroshot ui

Open http://127.0.0.1:4173/ui/. Profiles edits graphs and runtime settings; Runs shows live runs and replays completed ones. Ctrl-C stops the UI server while active runs continue. Use --listen 127.0.0.1:4185 to choose another port.

To inspect runs on a configured target while keeping profiles local:

zeroshot ui --target docker

Replace docker with your target's name, or platform after signing in. Profiles use ZEROSHOT_CONFIG_DIR; local run history uses ZEROSHOT_STATE_DIR. To start a saved local profile:

zeroshot run --title "My task" --profile local:my-profile --input input.json

See monitoring and replay or building the UI from source.

docs.title: Connect zeroshot Platform
docs.text:
zeroshot target login platform

Choose your organization in the browser, then add --target platform to run commands. The Platform docs cover accounts and saved connections. For self-hosting, see Targets.

docs.title: Update
docs.text:
zeroshot update

This updates the executable and unchanged managed skills. It preserves edited skills and reports conflicts by path. If skills are missing after upgrading through an older updater, run the command again. See update behavior for verification and failures.

For an npm installation, this replaces the bundled executables in place. npm's package metadata keeps the version originally installed, so npm list --global can show an older version than zeroshot --version. Reinstall through npm to bring its recorded version up to date.

Versions 10.4.0 through 10.8.0 cannot update themselves: their updater rejects the bundled sidecar with release archive contains unexpected entry restic (restic.exe on Windows). Reinstall once through npm; subsequent updates can use zeroshot update:

npm install --global @the-open-engine-company/zeroshot@latest

Updates preserve Active Memory storage.

docs.title: Agent skills
docs.text:
The installer adds zeroshot, zeroshot-plan, zeroshot-graph-design and zeroshot-memory-init for Codex, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot and Pi. No per-project setup is needed.

To install or update only the executables:

ZEROSHOT_SKIP_SKILLS=1 npm install --global @the-open-engine-company/zeroshot
ZEROSHOT_SKIP_SKILLS=1 zeroshot update

In PowerShell, set $env:ZEROSHOT_SKIP_SKILLS = '1' before either command. Existing skills remain untouched. Keep the variable in your shell configuration to preserve this choice across updates. See managed skills for paths and removal.

docs.title: GitHub Copilot
docs.text: For local GitHub-backed runs, sign in with copilot login. Contained runs need a user token with Copilot Requests permission; a GitHub App installation token cannot replace it. Copilot authentication covers BYOK and token refresh.

docs.title: Other installation paths
docs.text:
• Native archives include checksums.
  • The Python SDK bundles the matching executable and needs Python 3.11 or newer.
  • The Docker target runs zeroshot as a persistent service.

docs.title: Use a local graph as an ACP agent
docs.text: zeroshot acp is an experimental stdio endpoint that presents one saved local profile as an Agent Client Protocol (ACP) agent. Each ACP prompt runs the complete graph once, while the ACP session keeps the working folder and node provider sessions alive between prompts. Plain folders are accepted; a folder inside a Git checkout resolves to its root. The working folder must be disjoint from the active zeroshot state directory.

docs.title: Profile contract
docs.text:
The ACP preview accepts a deliberately narrow profile:

  • The graph input is one required string field named task.
  • Every success node returns one required string field named response.
  • Map nodes and Git delivery nodes aren't accepted.
  • Every executable node has an agent runtime binding with sessionScope set to node_instance.
  • Runtime connections aren't accepted. Registered local harnesses use their native login and configuration.
  • Agent nodes may mix registered harness lanes.

These limits keep one ACP turn equivalent to one ordinary local run; the graph compiler, reducer, provider adapters, and run ledger stay unchanged.

Save the graph and runtime as a local profile:

zeroshot profile set acp-worker \
  --graph graph.json \
  --runtime-config runtime.json

A minimal runtime has one node binding:

{
  "harness": "codex",
  "provider": "openai",
  "size": "medium",
  "nodes": {
    "worker": {
      "kind": "agent",
      "model": "PROVIDER_MODEL_ID",
      "sessionScope": "node_instance"
    }
  }
}

The corresponding graph has a task input, writes the worker's response into state, then returns it from the success node:

{
  "profile": "openengine.graph.full/v1",
  "initialInput": {
    "kind": "record",
    "fields": {
      "task": { "type": { "kind": "string" }, "required": true }
    }
  },
  "policy": { "policy": "policy.native-v2@1", "default": "deny" },
  "root": {
    "kind": "seq",
    "name": "root",
    "state": {
      "kind": "record",
      "fields": {
        "task": { "type": { "kind": "string" }, "required": true },
        "response": { "type": { "kind": "string" }, "required": true }
      }
    },
    "children": [
      {
        "kind": "step",
        "name": "worker",
        "worker": "agent.worker@1",
        "instructions": "Complete the task and return a concise response.",
        "input": {
          "kind": "record",
          "fields": {
            "task": { "type": { "kind": "string" }, "required": true }
          }
        },
        "output": {
          "kind": "record",
          "fields": {
            "response": { "type": { "kind": "string" }, "required": true }
          }
        },
        "inputBindings": [
          {
            "target": ["task"],
            "value": { "source": "state", "path": ["task"] }
          }
        ],
        "writeBindings": [
          {
            "target": ["response"],
            "value": {
              "node": "worker",
              "channel": "out",
              "path": ["response"]
            }
          }
        ],
        "attempts": 1
      },
      {
        "kind": "succeed",
        "name": "done",
        "output": {
          "kind": "record",
          "fields": {
            "response": { "type": { "kind": "string" }, "required": true }
          }
        },
        "bindings": [
          {
            "target": ["response"],
            "value": { "source": "state", "path": ["response"] }
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "promotedStatePaths": []
  }
}

docs.title: Start the endpoint
docs.text:
Configure the ACP client to launch the saved profile:

zeroshot acp --profile local:acp-worker

The command checks that each registered lane's executable is on PATH, as a local run does. Each session checks when it opens, against that session's workspace, and a missing executable fails session/new with an invalid-params error that names the lane and executable. If every PATH entry is absolute, the command also checks at startup. An empty or relative entry resolves against the directory the harness starts in, which is known only per session, so then the startup check is skipped.

ACP owns standard input and standard output for the lifetime of the process. Diagnostics go to standard error. The process accepts one active ACP session, doesn't implement session loading, and rejects MCP servers or extra workspace directories.

The client sends one nonempty ACP text block per prompt. zeroshot maps it to {"task":"..."} and streams the successful response as an agent message. The prompt response includes zeroshot-specific metadata with the durable run ID and raw graph output:

{
  "zeroshot": {
    "runId": "01...",
    "rawOutput": { "response": "..." }
  }
}

rawOutput is zeroshot's JSON form of the graph's terminal result, before ACP turns it into an agent message. Success is {"response":"..."}; an authored fail node is {"failed":"REASON"}.

Use that run ID with the ordinary read commands:

zeroshot status RUN_ID
zeroshot logs RUN_ID

Each prompt also appears in zeroshot ui as a normal local run, including its graph and retained history.

docs.title: Session and run lifetime
docs.text:
The ACP session takes one workspace lease and pins the workspace's filesystem identity. Losing either one stops the active turn as runtime_lost and rejects later prompts. Each prompt gets a fresh run ID, controller lock, SQLite ledger, and supervisor lifecycle, so it remains visible after the ACP session closes.

Provider sessions use stable graph-node slots within the outer ACP session. A clean node completion can therefore resume the same native harness session on the next prompt. Closing the ACP session cancels an active prompt, waits for it to settle, closes every provider session, and releases the workspace lease. session/cancel force-stops only the current durable turn and returns ACP's cancelled stop reason.

Authored graph failures are normal turn results: the agent emits a failure message and records the failure under rawOutput. When recorded failure context is available, the message includes the bounded foreground failure summary and the zeroshot logs RUN_ID command. Without recorded context, the message remains Zeroshot run failed: REASON. Admission, storage, or supervisor faults return a generic ACP internal error and write the safe diagnostic to standard error.

docs.title: Active Memory
docs.text:
Active Memory carries useful lessons from one run to the next. It saves guidance about costly mistakes and recurring work, then supplies relevant lessons when an agent encounters related code or runs the same graph again. It is enabled by default.

After the main graph finishes, a postmortem reviews the evidence, updates existing lessons and proposes new ones. Workers do not write directly to memory. Routine summaries and generic advice do not qualify as lessons.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Add these optional fields to your runtime JSON alongside harness, provider, size and nodes:

{
  "activeMemory": {
    "repository": true,
    "graph": true,
    "nodeInjectionTokens": 16000,
    "hookInjectionTokens": 8000
  },
  "globalAgents": {
    "postmortem": {
      "enabled": true,
      "sourceNode": "worker",
      "timeoutMs": 600000
    }
  }
}
  • Set repository or graph to false to stop reading and collecting lessons for that scope. Set both to false to disable Active Memory.
  • Set postmortem.enabled to false to keep reading saved lessons without updating them.
  • nodeInjectionTokens limits graph guidance per node invocation; hookInjectionTokens limits repository recall per tool callback. They default to 16000 and 8000 approximate tokens and each accepts 1–64000. One approximate token permits four UTF-8 bytes, including formatting. There is no cumulative conversation or run budget.
  • sourceNode selects the agent whose model, provider and connections the postmortem uses. Omit it to use the first worker, or the first agent verifier if there is no worker.
  • timeoutMs defaults to ten minutes and accepts 1–600000 milliseconds. Startup, investigation and all batches and retries share that deadline. Completed specialist work can publish after another specialist times out; an incomplete maintenance specialist publishes none of its decisions.

budgetBytes is replaced by the two injection limits; remove it from saved runtime JSON when upgrading.

These settings apply per run, so saved profiles can use different policies. Postmortem model usage counts toward the run total. An ordinary postmortem failure appears in the logs and does not change the main graph's result.

docs.title: Indexing and retrieval
docs.text:
Repository lessons match file paths, folders, identifiers and keyword groups. Graph lessons belong to a particular compiled graph and node; changing the graph creates a new scope. Lessons do not transfer automatically across graph versions.

Each run reads a snapshot of memory. New lessons become available to future runs. Matching makes no model calls. An ID/revision is supplied once per provider conversation; compaction does not reset this deduplication. Each matching injection gets its own context limit.

Repository lessons arrive through harness hooks. Disabled hooks can prevent delivery; scripts that hide their file paths can miss matches. Advice cannot change a tool call already issued, and receipt of a lesson does not prove the model followed it. See the matching and delivery rules for details.

docs.title: Storage and backups
docs.text:
Local runs share a database outside your checkouts, with separate repository scopes:

Platform Default database Linux / macOS ~/.local/state/zeroshot/active-memory/lessons.sqlite3 Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\zeroshot\state\active-memory\lessons.sqlite3

On Unix, XDG_STATE_HOME changes the base directory. ZEROSHOT_STATE_DIR takes precedence on all platforms and selects STATE_DIR/active-memory/lessons.sqlite3. Changing either variable selects a store; it does not move existing lessons.

A direct Docker target uses <target-storage>/active-memory/lessons.sqlite3, shared by its submitters with repository scopes. Preserve its storage volume when recreating the container. Local and target stores do not synchronize automatically. ACP integration is not supported.

Executable updates and normal run cleanup preserve memory. There are no automatic backups or built-in undo for changed or retired lessons. To back up or move it, stop all zeroshot processes using the store and copy the whole active-memory/ directory, including SQLite journal files. Restore it while those processes are stopped.

docs.title: Initialize from local history
docs.text:
Ask your agent to use the zeroshot-memory-init skill to learn from completed local runs. zeroshot update installs the skill; if it is missing after upgrading through an older updater, run the update again.

The skill inventories local history across repositories, discovers lessons, checks them against current source and publishes them together. Keep the selected checkouts stable during its final review and publication. It does not clone repositories, pull changes or change branches. Docker and Platform history are outside this workflow.

The skill uses this resumable command:

zeroshot memory init --directory /path/to/session
zeroshot memory init --directory /path/to/session --ignore-repos owner/repo,other-repo --ignore-graphs autoresearch,GRAPH_HASH

Choose a session directory outside checkouts. Ignore values must match inventory aliases exactly; saved exclusions apply when resuming. Unavailable checkouts and unusable runs are reported as exclusions. phase: complete returns the publication receipt; repeating a completed session does not publish twice.

See history initialization for alias matching, repository identity checks and interruption recovery.

docs.title: Concurrent maintenance and hosting
docs.text: Concurrent runs check lesson revisions before publishing, so stale updates cannot overwrite newer advice. Hosting integrations must explicitly provide a memory namespace and enforce its access. See memory lifecycle and storage for maintenance, evidence and host contracts.

docs.title: Review a PR in depth
docs.text: The code-review template reviews a pull request with parallel specialist reviewers, verifies their findings, and posts them as one Markdown comment. It takes the same input as pr-review and publishes through the same comment delivery. pr-review reproduces the changed behavior through the full local stack and posts a short verdict. code-review reads the change and reports every verified finding with its location, severity and suggested fix. It does not install dependencies or start applications, services or browsers.

docs.title: What the graph does
docs.text:
triage                 summary and at most six review units
discover (parallel)
  per unit:            two broad reviews, a depth review, a design review
  whole change:        logic, state, contracts, error paths, claims
finalize (parallel)
  per unit:            merge, try to disprove and rewrite the unit's findings
  remaining files:     the same for findings outside every unit
report                 final findings → one Markdown comment
deliver                native comment publication

Triage summarizes the change and splits its files into review units of a size one reviewer can examine carefully, keeping files that must be read together in the same unit. Four reviewers then examine every unit: two independent broad reviews, a depth review that builds a concrete failing scenario for each defect, and a design review that compares the code with the rest of the codebase. At the same time, five reviewers each hunt one kind of failure across the whole change. The claims reviewer also checks every acceptance criterion in the linked issues, unless the PR or the caller declares a partial implementation.

For every unit, a finalizer merges duplicate findings for the unit's files, tries to disprove each one against the real callers, guards and configuration, and rewrites the survivors with exact line ranges. Another finalizer does the same for findings outside every unit. The report agent orders the final findings by severity and writes the comment. The native publisher posts it after every agent has settled. The native header records the captured revisions once.

Every agent is read-only: it inspects the checkout and the diff of the admitted head against its merge base with the captured base revision, without changing tracked files. A change with N units runs 5N + 8 agent executions. A crashed agent is retried once. Any other agent failure, or a triage result with more units than the maps allow, stops the run before publication. Finding problems is a successful review.

docs.title: Prepare the runtime and credentials
docs.text:
The supplied runtime plan splits the agents across Claude Code and Codex, so that each unit and the whole change are reviewed by both model families. Save it as runtime.json and pass it through --runtime-config. It needs a Claude Code and a Codex login. Model choices remain in the caller's runtime plan rather than the graph, so a plan with other models, or a uniform runtime through --uniform-runtime-config, works as well.

The supplied plan sets workspaceCheckpoints: false for local reviews, skipping file snapshots and the Restic dependency. History, structured outputs, logs and comment receipts remain durable. A failed run can restart against its retained checkout, but cannot resume from a workspace snapshot. Set the same field in a uniform runtime file to use this policy with --uniform-runtime-config.

Comment delivery uses the github connection's GH_TOKEN, as for pr-review. Publication credentials belong to the native node and are not declared on the review agents.

docs.title: Run the review
docs.text:
Select a clean checkout already at the PR head. zeroshot refuses a mismatch instead of switching or resetting the worktree.

zeroshot run --title "Code review PR 123" \
  --template code-review \
  --task-from https://github.com/OWNER/REPOSITORY/pull/123 \
  --runtime-config runtime.json \
  --cwd /path/to/pr-checkout \
  --submission-key code-review-pr-123

--validate-only prepares and validates without executing agents. For hosted execution, set workspaceCheckpoints to true (or remove the field) before adding --target platform; named targets currently reject checkpoint opt-out. Source comes from URL resolution, so a client checkout is unnecessary.

docs.title: Input and result
docs.text:
The input and result match pr-review. --task-from captures {url, context} with the PR title and body, the complete context.reviewScope, and the linked issues. Optional caller instructions can narrow the review or declare a partial implementation. Like pr-review, the template requires comment delivery. The result retains the comment receipt, and each agent's findings stay in run history.

With prepared JSON passed through --input, the local checkout's upstream must name the captured PR base branch, for example origin/main. --task-from supplies that source identity itself.

docs.title: GitHub and GitLab delivery
docs.text:
GitHub.com, GitHub Enterprise, and GitLab use the same delivery nodes for PR/MR creation, merging, and issue or review comments.

Service Minimum version API credential GitHub.com / Enterprise Cloud (*.ghe.com) Hosted service GH_TOKEN GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.2 GH_TOKEN GitLab.com / self-managed GitLab 19.5.1 GITLAB_TOKEN

Instances must be publicly reachable over HTTPS with trusted TLS. Older or unidentifiable servers fail version checks. Use a web base without a trailing slash, including any GitLab installation prefix (such as https://gitlab.example/install). GitHub uses a root web URL.

docs.title: Local setup
docs.text:
Local --push, --pr and --ship runs require a clean checkout before agents start. Commit, stash or remove staged, unstaged and unignored untracked changes named in the refusal. Finish or abort a pending merge first. Changed submodule commit pointers count; files inside submodules do not. Runs without Git delivery keep their normal behavior. Delivery shows Git's warning when a run adds an unregistered embedded repository, but permits the gitlink; register it as a submodule when others need to clone it.

GitHub delivery requires gh. GitLab needs glab only to reuse its native login. Sign in to the host you use:

gh auth login --hostname github.com
gh auth login --hostname ghe.example
glab auth login --hostname gitlab.com

Local delivery reuses the selected host's login when its connection is empty. Explicit or saved values take precedence; partial connections fail. Ambient tokens are bound to GH_HOST or GITLAB_HOST; without a selector they apply only to GitHub.com or GitLab.com. Other hosts, including *.ghe.com, require a matching selector, a per-host CLI login, or declared connection values. Use repo and read:org for a classic GitHub PAT, or api and write_repository for a GitLab PAT. Git fetch and push must also work.

GitHub.com and GitLab.com remotes identify themselves automatically. Other hosts need a configured gh/glab login or explicit selection; a host configured in both CLIs needs explicit selection:

zeroshot run --title "Example change" --input task.json \
  --template software-change --uniform-runtime-config runtime.json --pr \
  --source-provider source.gitlab --source-base-url https://gitlab.example/install
