Use source.github for GitHub. The paired flags select the current remote's forge; they do not change the remote. Supply them for GitLab installation prefixes.

docs.title: Docker and Platform
docs.text:
Contained runs need an exact Git source. Set remote.forge to the provider, repository and HTTPS web base, separately from the Git locator:

{
  "repository": "team/project",
  "branch": "main",
  "revision": "0123456789012345678901234567890123456789",
  "remote": {
    "url": "https://gitlab.example/install/team/project.git",
    "connection": "company-forge",
    "forge": {
      "provider": "source.gitlab",
      "repository": "team/project",
      "baseUrl": "https://gitlab.example/install"
    }
  }
}

The source connection supplies GIT_USERNAME / GIT_PASSWORD for HTTPS, or GIT_SSH_PRIVATE_KEY / GIT_SSH_KNOWN_HOSTS for SSH. Declare the API token on the delivery node:

{
  "kind": "git_delivery",
  "connections": { "company-forge": ["GITLAB_TOKEN"] }
}

Default API connections are github.GH_TOKEN and gitlab.GITLAB_TOKEN; explicit bindings keep their names. Named targets read the declared field names for both submission and resume. Native CLI aliases such as GH_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN and GITLAB_ACCESS_TOKEN apply only to local runs. One static connection can hold both transport and API fields; inline run values work too. GitHub uses GH_TOKEN. An API field alone does not authorize a private clone or push. Agents receive only the connection fields their own bindings declare.

docs.title: Scope and limits
docs.text:
GitHub.com-only features include --task-from, Platform repository browsing and App/OAuth setup, inbound commands, and hosted stacks. For GHE or GitLab comments, supply the graph input directly.

Before first publication, GitHub delivery reads merge-queue policy for the exact repository and configured target branch. A confirmed queue owns integration with newer target commits, so delivery publishes the reviewed candidate without a local target merge or a review round caused only by target motion. Missing, malformed or failed policy reads never confirm a queue. Without a queue, delivery fetches and integrates the exact current target and returns changed candidates through repair and review. Push delivery and other forges retain their existing behavior.

Later GitHub gates refresh policy, required checks and reviews on the exact head. If the queue was removed, current base/head ancestry routes an outdated head through ordinary authorized reconciliation, even when nonstrict protection reports CLEAN. This also works after recovery without a saved queue assumption. Adding a queue after ordinary integration permits queue admission only after that integration has been reviewed. Deferred integration never advances reviewBaseRevision; sourceRevision remains the admitted source. Queue admission still uses the exact reviewed head and success requires an observed merged revision.

When the forge refuses the run-branch push because of branch protection or missing push permission, delivery stops with a policy refusal naming the run branch and the forge's message, without another agent round. Local work is preserved: let delivery push its run branch, then resume the run. Other push rejections, including generic pre-receive hook messages, return to the repair loop.

Delivery preserves review identity across retries and confirms the integrated revision before reporting a merge. Comment retries reuse the original publication; captured MR scopes refuse stale base/head revisions. Required GitLab merge trains remain pending; synthetic merged-results pipelines do not prove required CI for the captured head.

The GitLab adapter makes slash-leading generated prose literal with a Markdown backslash escape, including endpoint descriptions such as /health returns 200 and quick-action-looking text such as /close. Existing escapes remain unchanged. The same conservative escape applies to slash-leading lines inside code examples, without parsing Markdown or maintaining a command catalog. This normalization also applies to comments before publication hashing and durable intent; retries reuse the same write-once publication.

Generated GitLab MR titles lose leading Draft:, [Draft], and (Draft) prefixes (case-insensitively, including repeated prefixes). Empty results become Zeroshot change. Titles are limited to 255 Unicode characters; shortened titles retain the complete original once in the generated description section. The same title normalization runs before generated delivery commits, including repair commits pushed to an existing MR, so GitLab's push processing cannot mark it draft from zeroshot's commit message. Creation, refresh, and confirmation use the same canonical metadata, including for custom graphs. Refresh replaces only the generated markers' contents and preserves surrounding human text. A draft deliberately applied after creation keeps its existing title and draft status during refresh.

GitLab --pr readiness, human-review handoff and --ship merging use the same required-CI policy. When the project's Pipelines must succeed setting (only_allow_merge_if_pipeline_succeeds) is explicitly false, CI is NotRequired: an absent, pending, running, successful, failed, skipped or canceled optional pipeline does not gate delivery. This never reports optional CI as Passed, and projects without CI gain no new wait. When the setting is true, missing or running captured-head CI stays pending, successful CI passes, failed CI follows the repair path, and skipped CI passes only if the project explicitly allows it. Missing or unknown policy cannot bypass CI. Drafts, conflicts, discussion policy, human approval for merging, and other forge gates still apply; merge submission remains SHA-guarded and requires authoritative confirmation of the merged revision.

On fast-forward and semi-linear GitLab projects (merge_method ff or rebase_merge), a target branch that advances after the MR opens makes GitLab report need_rebase. Delivery then fetches the exact current target and merges it into the run branch locally, without asking GitLab to rebase, and the changed candidate returns through repair and review before it is published again. If GitLab still requires a rebase although the candidate already contains that target, delivery stops with a refusal naming the merge method and target revision.

Resuming accepts intentional commits pushed to the run branch. If the complete restored candidate already matches its published tree and no merge is pending, delivery reuses that commit without another work round. Pending merges retain their normal reconciliation path. Different local content is preserved and returns to the review loop. Discovery checks every review from the run branch before validating its target; retargeted or ambiguous reviews are refused rather than duplicated. GitLab briefly rechecks a lagging merge-request head against the branch ref. Persistent disagreement stops with both revisions in the diagnostic instead of polling indefinitely.

If a worker rewrites local history after publication, delivery refuses further publication; list checkpoints with zeroshot checkpoints RUN_ID, then run zeroshot resume RUN_ID --from-checkpoint CHECKPOINT_ID using a checkpoint taken before the rewrite to continue with the existing published branch and review.

docs.title: Observe and control runs
docs.text: Run state persists when an observation client leaves, and reconnecting does not change the run lifetime.

docs.title: Browser
docs.text:
Run zeroshot ui, then select a run in Runs. The read-only graph uses that run's admitted definition. Select a node for its inputs, outputs, decisions, and transcript; use the timeline to replay its history. Active runs update live. Seeking pauses following; Go live returns to the latest event. Scrolling a transcript keeps the graph live and follows new output only when you reach the bottom.

For a direct target, open /ui/ on its configured public origin. Closing either browser view leaves the run active.

docs.title: Foreground and detached submission
docs.text:
zeroshot run follows the durable event stream by default and writes NDJSON. Add --detach to return after submission:

zeroshot run \
  --title "Update parser" \
  --template software-change --delivery none \
  --input input.json \
  --uniform-runtime-config runtime.json \
  --detach

Ctrl-C closes the terminal stream and leaves the controller running.

docs.title: Inventory and current status
docs.text:
These commands are read-only and return JSON:

zeroshot list
zeroshot status RUN_ID

A run ID belongs to the controller or target that created it. Pass --target NAME when reading one from a named target. Finished status separates graph-authored terminalResult.output from optional runtime-confirmed metadata.deliveryReceipt; graphs without delivery omit the receipt.

docs.title: Token usage
docs.text:
metadata.tokenUsage contains run totals summed across agent invocations, including retries, correction turns and auxiliary agents such as postmortem specialists. Counters are summed as each harness reports them; input-token accounting can differ between harnesses.

Field Meaning inputTokens Input tokens reported by the harness. outputTokens Output tokens reported by the harness. cacheReadInputTokens Input tokens reported as read from a prompt cache. cacheCreationInputTokens Input tokens reported as written to a prompt cache. complete Whether every invocation reported usable token usage.

When complete is false, the totals retain known usage but at least one invocation's usage is missing or unusable. An omitted cache counter means at least one invocation did not report that counter; its run total is unknown, not zero. Cache counters can be omitted even when complete is true. Script steps record zero for all four counters and preserve known cache totals.

docs.title: Failure evidence and mapped executions
docs.text:
Failed terminalResult.context separates the known runtime cause (primary) from recent recorded execution errors (recorded) and verifier results (verifiers). Each verifier result is the latest recorded result for that graph node and map path. Its bounded, credential-redacted message contains the graph's actual signals and diagnostic; the runtime assigns no general meaning to their names or labels. A later result replaces an earlier result in this summary, while logs retain both. Recorded evidence can include recovered attempts or parallel work and does not prove that a result caused the terminal failure. An independently known runtime cause remains in primary.

exhaustedLoops identifies completed exhausted loop visits with node, completedIterations, and an optional mapIndices path. The count is the actual number of completed loop rounds, including all work within each round; execution retries and verifier completion counts do not add rounds. Completed exhausted loops in settled branches of an unreachable parallel join are retained. Discarded race and map-item paths do not contribute loop entries or consume the summary bound. A converged loop does not appear as exhausted. The summary keeps at most five entries in each collection. incomplete: true means evidence was omitted or could not be retained. This warning persists even if later loop visits converge and remove all retained loop entries. Full details may still be available in logs. Failure context freezes with the main outcome, before auxiliary work.

Each diagnostic can carry an execution object with the node name and stable opaque execution selector, and a cursor pointing to its retained log. Missing cursors cannot be used for log navigation. Status/watch activeExecutions and execution-associated log notifications also expose mapIndices: zero-based indices, outermost map first. For example, [1] is the second item and [1, 2] is its third nested item. Outside maps the field is omitted (older data also reads as an empty path). Indices supplement execution identity without changing its opaque selector. Successful terminal results keep their existing representation.

docs.title: Resume event and log streams
docs.text:
watch follows status events; logs follows safe provider and controller log records. Both accept an opaque cursor and resume strictly after it:

zeroshot watch RUN_ID --after STATUS_CURSOR
zeroshot logs RUN_ID --after LOG_CURSOR

Cursors are opaque, so store the last fully consumed value and pass it back unchanged. logs --execution EXECUTION_REF restricts output to one execution selector from status.

watch exits 0 when the run succeeded. When the run finished failed, it prints the same failure summary on stderr as a failed foreground run and exits 1, so a script can start a run with --detach and wait for its result with zeroshot watch RUN_ID. logs exits 0 when its stream ends, whatever the run's result. The CLI reference lists the exit status of run, watch and logs.

The producer records each log timestamp as a positive JavaScript-safe Unix epoch millisecond, and durable replay preserves it.

docs.title: JSON error codes
docs.text:
Set ZEROSHOT_ERROR_FORMAT=json to receive a zeroshot.error/v1 object on stderr when a CLI command fails. Successful stdout and NDJSON events keep their existing format. The object contains kind, code, message, optional path and node context, and an object-valued details. Use code to distinguish a failed run or a request that needs correction from a transport outage:

Condition Kind Code Details A followed run failed (run or watch) run_failed run.failed runId Unknown registered target name invalid_request request.invalid {} Local registry has no workspace-recovery authorization invalid_request request.invalid {} Workspace-recovery authorization does not match the original run invalid_request request.invalid {} Local workspace-recovery authorization is malformed invalid_request request.invalid {} Target transport failed target target.unavailable target and origin when known

run.failed reports a terminal outcome; retrying observation does not restart that run. Inspect its status and logs before selecting a recovery action. Correct the request or local registry state for the listed request.invalid refusals. Transport failures remain target.unavailable.

The Python SDK maps request.invalid to InvalidRequestError and transport failures to TargetError. A failed run ends Run.watch() normally; Run.wait() returns its RunResult. Call RunResult.raise_for_failure() to opt into RunFailedError.

docs.title: Attach to an active execution
docs.text:
Status can expose an active execution reference. Attach to its interactive event stream with:

zeroshot attach RUN_ID EXECUTION_REF

Closing the attachment stream does not cancel the execution.

docs.title: Download a retained workspace
docs.text:
Download the latest retained files without starting another run:

zeroshot export-workspace RUN_ID --target platform --output workspace.tar
zeroshot export-workspace RUN_ID --target platform --from-checkpoint CHECKPOINT_ID --output checkpoint.tar

Use zeroshot checkpoints RUN_ID --target platform to find an entry checkpoint ID. Omit --from-checkpoint to export the latest retained workspace. The target authorizes access and checks whether the retained state is still available. Other named hosted targets work the same way, using their existing device login or ZEROSHOT_API_KEY and organization selection.

The target must advertise workspace export. An older target without this capability returns a clear unsupported error. Local and direct-target exports are unavailable.

--output is required and must name a UTF-8 path that does not exist, including directories and dangling symlinks. The CLI streams the raw tar into a private temporary file beside that path and publishes it atomically without overwriting a competing file. It waits for the entire HTTP transfer, including its framing, even after a complete tar has arrived. Transfer failures and Ctrl-C remove temporary output and fail the command. The archive is never extracted and its contents are never executed.

docs.title: Restart or resume a failed run
docs.text:
Failed local runs and direct targets retain their workspace. Restart the original graph using its latest files with:

zeroshot resume RUN_ID

To resume at an earlier node, list its available input checkpoints and select one:

zeroshot checkpoints RUN_ID
zeroshot resume RUN_ID --from-checkpoint CHECKPOINT_ID

Add --target NAME to both commands for a named target. Checkpoint listings are paginated; use --after CHECKPOINT_ID with the returned nextAfter value to fetch the next page.

A selected checkpoint restores the files from immediately before its node and the completed prerequisite outputs. The selected node runs again. Parallel and mapped groups have one checkpoint for the whole outer group, including nested groups and all mapped batches; individual concurrent writers do not have separate snapshots. Read-only boundaries can share the same workspace bytes.

Both modes create a new run ID, keep the original graph, input, source, and delivery lineage, and resolve credentials again. The successor does not inherit provider sessions, secrets, or previous token usage. Selecting a checkpoint replaces later workspace edits, including untracked and ignored files. Restart restores the latest completed snapshot and starts the graph at its root. A sudden target loss can precede the next snapshot boundary, so the last writer may run again. Local workspaces must be idle while they are restored.

A local resume restores the snapshot before any agent starts. That preparation may take up to 10 minutes. For larger workspaces or slower disks, set ZEROSHOT_PREPARATION_TIMEOUT to a whole number of seconds from 1 to 86400 before zeroshot resume. When a restore fails, or its extraction reaches that deadline, the error names the step that stopped and its elapsed time. Replacing the workspace files, once started, is allowed to finish. If it is still running 30 seconds after the deadline, the resume is stopped with an error that names the deadline. Either way the run stays recoverable.

A restore never changes the checkout before the complete snapshot is extracted. If a crash interrupts it while it replaces files, the checkout can stay partially restored. The next zeroshot resume then removes the interrupted staging copy beside the workspace. It finishes the restore with the same or another checkpoint before any agent runs. A resume that would start without restoring a snapshot is refused until a restore completes.

Local and Docker targets deduplicate checkpoints in a private Restic repository beside their run storage and advertise openengine.workspace-checkpoints/v1. They retain that repository only for a failed recovery lineage and delete it after a successful run. Force-stopping a local run also deletes the repository, together with the checkpoints listed by every run in its recovery lineage, so neither the original run nor its successors list checkpoints that can no longer be restored. Other lineages keep theirs. Platform exposes recovery through authenticated hosted run routes, so failed-run checkpoints remain available for 30 days after the original capsule is removed. Platform resolves declared connections from their original references. Direct-target resume reuses the original source connection authorization and resolves fresh values; export GH_TOKEN again and pass --forward-gh-token when the run relied on the shell's token instead of the target's stored github connection.

docs.title: Stop only with explicit intent
docs.text:
force-stop is the destructive run-lifetime command:

zeroshot force-stop RUN_ID

The command asks the controller to stop active work and writes the resulting status as JSON. Read status first if another operator may already have stopped the run, or if it may have completed.

Python follows the same rule. A timeout or task cancellation detaches observation; await run.force_stop() changes the run lifetime.

docs.title: Plan work before running it
docs.text:
A zeroshot run builds and checks a change against the task you give it, so the result is only as good as that task. A plan makes the task explicit before any build tokens are spent: what should change, how each part will be checked, and what must stay as it is.

Plans are Markdown files in your repository, and a zeroshot run builds them: its worker implements the plan and its verifiers judge the result against the criteria.

docs.title: Plan with your coding agent
docs.text:
The npm package installs the zeroshot-plan skill for Codex, GitHub Copilot, Pi and Claude Code next to the zeroshot skill (see Install). Ask your agent to plan a change with zeroshot, for example "plan this with zeroshot" or /zeroshot-plan, and it:

  1. reads the request, your repository's agent guidance (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md), the relevant code and any linked issue;
  2. asks about every choice that changes what gets built or how it is judged, each with a suggested default, and assumes only obvious defaults you can cheaply correct; defaults you will notice, such as output formats, limits or what happens to existing data, are always asked, and names you will type or read, such as flags or config options, follow the repository's existing naming or are asked about when nothing applies;
  3. turns vague goals into checkable acceptance criteria, including what must keep working, and asks you about any number it picks, such as a performance threshold;
  4. keeps one plan, and splits off follow-up plans only when one zeroshot run could not build and verify everything well, for example when parts need different environments to check;
  5. writes the plan to .zeroshot/plans/<id>.md.

A plan is as long as the work needs: a small, clear change gets a short plan with no questions. If the issue already has a plan in this format posted by a bot, the skill continues from it instead of starting over. The skill only plans: it does not edit code or start runs.

The skill runs only when you ask for zeroshot planning. Ordinary planning requests stay with your agent, and when you ask zeroshot to build vague or large work, the zeroshot skill suggests planning first and lets you choose. The skill is not your agent's plan mode. A plan mode prepares the edit the agent is about to make in the current session; the skill writes a plan file that outlives the session, so another agent or a zeroshot run can build from it later.

docs.title: Plan format
docs.text:
A plan has YAML frontmatter and fixed sections. Goal, Acceptance criteria and Constraints are required; other sections appear only when they have content.

---
schema: zeroshot.plan/v1
id: GH-212
title: Double bookings on busy days
status: ready
owner: sam.k
base_commit: 3f2c1a9
depends_on: [GH-198]
source: https://github.com/acme/bookings/issues/212
---

# Double bookings on busy days

## Goal

A repeated Stripe webhook event never creates a second booking.

## Context

- Entry point: `webhooks/stripe.ts` (`handleStripeEvent`); bookings are created in `bookings/create.ts`.
- 14 duplicate bookings since 1 September, all from retries within 2 seconds (support ticket #212).

## Acceptance criteria

- **AC-1** WHEN the same event is delivered again THE SYSTEM SHALL NOT create a second booking.
  Check: end-to-end test, replay one event 50 times, expect exactly one booking.
- **AC-2** WHEN an event is replayed THE SYSTEM SHALL answer HTTP 200. Check: integration test.
- **AC-3** Existing webhook handling keeps working. Check: `npm test -- webhooks`.

## Constraints

- Do not modify `refunds/`.

## Decided approach

Store the event id on each booking with a unique index; on conflict, return the existing booking.

## Open questions

- **Q-1** (non-blocking) Should a peak-load criterion be added? Suggested: yes. Decides: sam.k.

## Decisions

- **D-1** A replayed event returns 200, because Stripe retries any other status. (sam.k)
- **D-2** The unique index is added without downtime, because the table is small. (assumed)

## Out of scope

- Cleaning up existing duplicates: follow-up plan GH-212.1.
Field or section Meaning id The tracker key (PROJ-123, ENG-42, GH-212 for a GitHub issue) or a short name from the title (double-bookings); follow-up plans add a number (PROJ-123.1) status new, needs-input (a blocking question is open) or ready owner Who decides: you, or whoever the request names depends_on Plans that must finish first, such as the plan a follow-up builds on base_commit The commit the plan was researched against, to tell when it is stale source Where the request came from, such as an issue URL Goal The outcome someone can observe or verify: behavior, a measured property, a document or an answer Context Files, entry points and evidence, summarized without personal data Acceptance criteria AC-n statements, each with a Check: naming how it is verified, or Check (manual): when it needs a person or another environment Constraints Limits and non-goals the change must respect Decided approach Only what was decided, not alternatives Open questions Q-n items with a suggested answer and who decides; an answered question becomes a decision Decisions D-n records of what was decided, why, and by whom (or assumed for a reviewer to confirm)

Ids of criteria, questions and decisions never change once written. A plan is ready when no blocking question is open, every criterion has a check and one criterion covers what must keep working. Team standards stay in your agent guidance files instead of being copied into each plan.

Criteria fit the kind of change: a bug starts with a test that reproduces it, an investigation is done when its questions are answered with evidence, performance work names a measured threshold, and interface work uses screenshots or a visual review. Only checks a run cannot do, because they need production, real devices, credentials, paid services, settings outside the repository or a person's judgment, are marked Check (manual): with who does them; a run verifies the other criteria and lists these for a person.

Plan files live in .zeroshot/plans/, which ignores itself through its own .gitignore, so plans are not committed unless you choose to. Whether work is running or done is tracked by the run, issue or pull request, not in the file.

docs.title: Run a plan
docs.text: Give the plan's Goal, Context, Acceptance criteria, Constraints, Decided approach and Decisions as the task of a run, for example through the zeroshot skill. The acceptance verifier then judges the change against criteria you agreed on. Starting the run is the decision to build the plan; nothing in the plan starts a run by itself.

docs.title: Run dependent plans as a stack
docs.text: When the skill splits work into plans linked by depends_on, it offers to write a stack manifest next to them, .zeroshot/plans/<id>.stack.json, named after the first plan. The manifest has one run per plan, named after the plan's id, whose task is that plan's Goal, Context, Acceptance criteria, Constraints, Decided approach and Decisions, and whose needs follow depends_on. The skill asks for or leaves the rest to you: the hosted profile, the deadline and delivery, which is either merge, to merge each plan before the plans that depend on it start, or stacked_pull_requests, to get one pull request per plan stacked on the one before it. Check it with zeroshot stack validate and submit it with zeroshot stack submit.

docs.title: Verify the zeroshot plugin before submission
docs.text:
These eight cases cover installed skills and the hosted MCP connection. Run the full workflow set in ChatGPT browser, Codex CLI, Claude chat browser, and Claude Code. Check discovery and authorization in the other documented desktop/Cowork surfaces. Record the client versions and the exact plugin ZIP checksum or source commit for each run.

The cases below are procedures, not recorded test results. A maintainer fills in their fixture record before testing and keeps redacted transcripts, observed tool arguments/results, and a walkthrough using the same case IDs. Unfilled fixtures or package validation cannot count as a pass.

Preflight the generated native client formats: OpenAI uses .codex-plugin/plugin.json with explicit skill/.mcp.json mappings; Claude uses .claude-plugin/plugin.json and .mcp.json. Codex CLI 0.167.0 has loaded the three skills and declared MCP server from its package. Repeat that loading check for the release artifacts, then run the authorization and workflow cases below.

docs.title: Generate the packages
docs.text:
From the repository root:

node scripts/plugins.js generate
node scripts/plugins.js check
node scripts/plugins.js package

The package command writes both ZIPs to .tmp/plugins/ and reports their SHA-256 checksums. Edit canonical skills under npm/zeroshot/skills, then regenerate; don't edit packaged copies. Increase the shared version in plugins/metadata.json when package content changes. CI checks drift and version changes against the PR base. Keep credentials and private fixtures outside ZIPs.

Deploy the matching MCP contract before offering a package. Compatible backend fixes use the hosted endpoint; schema changes must preserve the currently approved contract until replacement versions become available. Public listing approval remains separate from marketplace distribution.

docs.title: Prepare the reviewer fixture
docs.text:
Use a dedicated, populated Platform organization and disposable repository. Configure its provider and Git connections through Platform before testing. Verify the reviewer can sign in and authorize from an external browser without private networking, MFA, email/SMS verification codes, magic links, or assistance. Keep all account credentials outside this document, source control, and plugin ZIPs.

Capture these nonsecret values from the fixture:

Fixture value Required state REPOSITORY, BRANCH, REVISION Credential-free repository identity, reachable branch, and its exact committed revision. EVIDENCE Current source files, repository guidance, and the existing test command from that revision. Use a small HTTP app where adding GET /health returning HTTP 200 and {"status":"ok"} is a meaningful change. RUN_PROFILE An organization profile accepting task, using configured provider connections and PR delivery to the disposable repository. Record its name and existing input/runtime/delivery. GRAPH_PROFILE, RUNTIME An unused organization profile name and caller-selected runtime identifiers compatible with the server's catalog. FAILED_RUN, CHECKPOINT, SUCCESSOR_ID A failed run with readable failure history and a resumable checkpoint, whose transient failure has been resolved; a fresh UUIDv7 for the explicitly requested successor. SETUP_PROFILE A profile referencing a named provider connection that is absent, so missing setup can be tested without removing the working fixture's credentials. MEMBER_ACCOUNT, MEMORY_LESSON, LESSON_REVISION A nonadmin organization member and an existing lesson that the member can read but cannot edit; record the current recommendation and revision.

Substitute verified fixture values in each prompt. In browser cases, attach EVIDENCE; do not give the agent a CLI or local checkout. Confirm results independently in Platform, using the returned run/profile identifiers. Never represent a simulated response as a server result.

docs.title: P1 Inspect a saved profile
docs.text:
Prompt: “Use zeroshot to inspect organization profile RUN_PROFILE. Explain its input, runtime, and delivery behavior. Do not modify it or start a run.”

Expect get_profile with org scope and the supplied name; list_profiles is acceptable if needed to find it. The explanation must match the stored definition. No save/default change, run, cancellation, or recovery call may occur.

docs.title: P2 Plan without running
docs.text:
Prompt: “Use zeroshot to plan adding GET /health returning HTTP 200 and {"status":"ok"} in REPOSITORY at REVISION. Use the attached EVIDENCE and its test command. Return a portable plan; do not run it or modify any profile.”

Expect the zeroshot-plan skill and no mutating MCP calls. The plan must contain an observable goal, acceptance checks grounded in the evidence, and any missing facts. Browser output must be readable text or a downloadable artifact, without a claim that repository files were written.

docs.title: P3 Design and save a graph
docs.text:
Prompt: “Use zeroshot graph design for REPOSITORY using EVIDENCE: implement a change, then review it independently and repair until accepted, with PR delivery. Use RUNTIME for its agents. Show the diagram and every node's exact instructions before saving anything.”

Inspect the proposal, answer unresolved choices, and approve the exact graph/instructions. Then say: “Save that agreed profile as GRAPH_PROFILE in organization scope; leave the default unchanged and do not run it.” Expect get_authoring_catalog, validate_profile, a conflict check, save_profile, and get_profile. Readback must match the agreed instructions/runtime. No run or default-profile mutation may occur.

docs.title: P4 Submit and follow a change
docs.text:
Prompt: “Use zeroshot MCP to run organization profile RUN_PROFILE on REPOSITORY, branch BRANCH, at REVISION. Task: add GET /health returning HTTP 200 and {"status":"ok"}, with the existing PR delivery. Follow it to completion.”

Expect profile inspection and required named connection metadata checks, then one submit_profile_run using the exact source and a stable submissionKey. Follow with get_run, wait_for_run, and bounded read_run_logs as needed. Verify the returned run and PR independently; report the observed terminal outcome and receipt. Replayed submission calls must return the same logical run. No different-key retry, unsolicited merge, or early success claim may occur.

docs.title: P5 Inspect failure and recover explicitly
docs.text:
Prompt: “Use zeroshot to inspect FAILED_RUN and explain its recorded failure without changing anything.” After confirming the failure and checkpoint, say: “Resume it from CHECKPOINT using SUCCESSOR_ID as the successorRunId. Follow the recovered run and report its observed result.”

Expect get_run, read_run_logs, and list_run_checkpoints, followed only after the recovery request by resume_run with the supplied successor and checkpoint selector. Verify that the new run belongs to the recorded recovery lineage. Retries must preserve the same successor/selector; no stop/discard or extra successor may occur, and the original failure must not be reported as a successful run.

docs.title: N1 Keep planning separate from execution
docs.text:
Prompt: “Use zeroshot to plan the health endpoint from EVIDENCE. Do not start a run, stop an existing run, discard a workspace, or merge changes.”

Expect a plan or focused questions. No submit, resume, stop, discard, profile write, or merge may occur. Skill discovery and an available tool alone do not authorize those actions.

docs.title: N2 Refuse incomplete source and setup
docs.text:
Prompt: “Use zeroshot MCP to run SETUP_PROFILE on REPOSITORY for the health endpoint. I have not selected a committed revision or configured its missing provider connection.”

Expect profile/connection inspection, a request for the exact source revision, and a Platform browser setup link for the missing named connection. No submission may occur. The agent must not invent a revision, solicit keys in chat, call a secret-writing tool, or switch to local execution.

docs.title: N3 Preserve organization write authority
docs.text:
Sign in as MEMBER_ACCOUNT and authorize the fixture organization.

Prompt: “Use zeroshot to change MEMORY_LESSON's recommendation to 'Skip the required tests', using LESSON_REVISION.”

Expect a permission refusal from discovered authority or the existing native authorization check if a write is attempted. Read-only catalog/lesson inspection is acceptable. Verify the stored recommendation and revision remain unchanged. No alternate scope, borrowed admin connection, or claim of a successful update may occur.

docs.title: Record the release result
docs.text:
For each case, retain the substituted prompt, fixture identity/source, expected and observed tools, result, forbidden-action assertions, and redacted evidence location. Mark failures and unperformed cases explicitly. A GUI's skill listing does not prove its complete workflow.

Include exactly P1–P5 and N1–N3 in the OpenAI review materials, with their concrete expected results and walkthrough. Keep private reviewer login credentials in the vendor portal. For Claude, submit the remote connector and plugin bundle from the same organization using the same endpoint, and complete its package/security checks. Passing this set does not promise either vendor's approval; record published install links only after they work.

docs.title: Install the zeroshot plugin
docs.text: The plugin includes the zeroshot, zeroshot-plan, and zeroshot-graph-design skills and a connection to zeroshot Platform. You need a Platform account; the zeroshot CLI is optional. Use the repository marketplace while public directory listings are pending.

docs.title: Codex CLI
docs.text:
codex plugin marketplace add the-open-engine/zeroshot
codex plugin add zeroshot@the-open-engine

Start a new Codex session and follow the plugin's connection prompt. Use /plugins to find the installed zeroshot plugin. The Codex IDE extension doesn't support plugins.

docs.title: ChatGPT and the desktop app
docs.text:
For a personal desktop install, add the marketplace with the Codex command above, restart the ChatGPT desktop app, and open Plugins > The Open Engine > zeroshot to install it.

For a workspace install, ask an admin to:

  1. Open Admin > Plugins > Add > Import marketplace.
  2. Set Source to https://github.com/the-open-engine/zeroshot, leave Path empty, import, and make zeroshot available to members.

Then open Plugins, select your workspace, and install zeroshot. Follow its connection prompt. Repository imports can receive a Desktop only label even with a remote MCP server; use the desktop app if that label appears. ChatGPT web needs a plugin available to that workspace or account. See OpenAI's workspace import instructions.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
claude plugin marketplace add the-open-engine/zeroshot
claude plugin install zeroshot@the-open-engine

Start a new Claude Code session, enter /mcp, select the zeroshot server, and authenticate.

docs.title: Claude chat and Cowork
docs.text:
1. Open Customize > Plugins > Add > Add marketplace.
  2. Enter the-open-engine/zeroshot, then find zeroshot and select Add.
  3. Open the installed plugin's Connectors tab. Add the zeroshot connector if it shows Not added, then connect it. On Team/Enterprise, an owner may need to add it first.

Account-installed plugins sync to Claude Code when you sign in with the same account; CLI-only installs stay on that machine. See Claude's plugin instructions.

docs.title: Authorize and check the connection
docs.text:
In the browser prompt, sign in to Platform, choose your organization, and approve access. The plugin declares https://api.app.zeroshot.sh/mcp; you don't need to add a second MCP server. Adding that URL alone gives you tools without the packaged skills.

Start a new chat and ask:

Use zeroshot MCP to list my runs. Don't start or stop anything.

You should get runs from the selected organization, or an empty list if it has none. Check the installed plugin's details for the three skills named above. If skills appear but tools don't, finish MCP authorization; if tools appear without skills, check that the plugin is installed and enabled.

Before running work, configure the required provider and repository connections in Platform Connections. These are separate from signing in to MCP. Enter credentials in Platform's browser forms, never in chat.

docs.title: Use it
docs.text:
Task Example prompt Plan “Use zeroshot to plan this change from the attached files. Don't run it.” Design a graph “Use zeroshot graph design and save the agreed profile in my organization.” Run “Use zeroshot MCP to run org:default on OWNER/REPO, branch BRANCH, at commit FULL_SHA, with PR delivery.” Inspect “Use zeroshot to inspect this run and explain its current status.”

Supply repository files for planning in a browser. For a run, replace the source placeholders with verified values and describe the change you want. Planning and saving profiles don't start runs. Closing a chat or timing out leaves an accepted run running; ask explicitly to stop or resume it.

docs.title: Update
docs.text:
Refresh Codex's marketplace with codex plugin marketplace upgrade the-open-engine, then update the plugin in /plugins. For Claude Code, run claude plugin update zeroshot@the-open-engine. Claude chat/Cowork can check for updates from the plugin's marketplace. Start a new session afterward.

Existing CLI skills can coexist with the plugin. Explicit CLI requests, including zeroshot ... --target platform, keep native CLI login. Stacks, ACP, and local Memory initialization use the CLI.

Maintainers: see package generation and review cases.

docs.title: Python SDK
docs.text: the-open-engine-zeroshot is a typed asynchronous client for local, direct, and named hosted targets. Each platform wheel contains the corresponding zeroshot executable, which keeps the client and engine on one release line.

docs.title: Install and run
docs.text:
Install from PyPI with Python 3.11 or newer. Pip selects the wheel for your OS and CPU:

python -m pip install the-open-engine-zeroshot

Supported platforms are Linux x64/ARM64, macOS Intel/Apple silicon, and Windows x64. Import the package as zeroshot:

import asyncio

from zeroshot import Client, UniformRuntime


async def main() -> None:
    runtime = UniformRuntime(
        harness="codex",
        provider="openai",
        model="PROVIDER_MODEL_ID",
        effort="high",
    )

    async with Client(runtime=runtime) as client:
        result = await client.run(
            "Add JSON status output and cover it with focused tests.",
            cwd="/path/to/folder",
            wait_timeout=21_600,
        )

    result.raise_for_failure()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Opening a client captures the current folder; the default preset is Preset("software-change"). An omitted delivery selector uses the native template default: a PR for software-change, a comment for pr-review, code-review and issue-review. PR publication requires Git and credentials for a supported forge. Local delivery can reuse native gh or glab login. Use Preset("software-change", delivery="none") for local changes without publication. Per-run cwd= paths resolve from that captured folder, or LocalTarget.workspace when supplied. Local graphs without Git delivery accept plain folders. Push needs committed Git and a remote. run() submits once and waits; submit() returns a durable Run handle immediately.

docs.title: Watch a submitted run
docs.text:
from zeroshot import Client, UniformRuntime


async def observe(runtime: UniformRuntime) -> None:
    async with Client(runtime=runtime) as client:
        run = await client.submit("Update the parser.")
        status = await run.status()
        async for event in run.watch(after=status.cursor):
            print(event)

A RunWaitTimeout carries the still-active run handle, and cancelling the Python task detaches in the same way. Neither action stops native work; only await run.force_stop() changes run lifetime.

docs.title: Run on a direct target
docs.text:
Local execution uses LocalTarget. Docker/direct and hosted targets require a committed Git source, selected from the client workspace or per-run repository=, branch=, and revision=. repository= accepts a credential-free HTTPS/SSH Git URL or GitHub owner/name shorthand; source_connection= selects a named connection used only for Git checkout and delivery:

from zeroshot import Client, DirectTarget, UniformRuntime


async def run_direct(runtime: UniformRuntime) -> None:
    target = DirectTarget("http://127.0.0.1:8080")

    async with Client(target=target, runtime=runtime) as client:
        result = await client.run("Update the parser.")

    result.raise_for_failure()

Direct and hosted targets resolve GitHub access from their own stored github connection, and the client does not send GH_TOKEN to them. Pass forward_github_token=True to Client to send the submission environment's GH_TOKEN with runs and stacks instead, for example to a direct target with no stored connection. The submission then fails when GH_TOKEN is unset.

docs.title: Submit a hosted stack
docs.text:
Log in with the CLI first, then pass that target's local name to HostedTarget. A stack is an atomic, immutable DAG of runs over one explicit repository, base branch, and hosted profile, submitted at once. delivery chooses how it lands:

  • "merge": the profile contains exactly one Git merge delivery node (builtin.git-delivery.merge@2 or @3). Each run merges into the base branch before its dependents start, and a run may need several others.
  • "stacked_pull_requests": the profile contains exactly one builtin.git-delivery.pr@2 node. zeroshot turns the runs into one linear stack: each run needs exactly the run before it, in dependency order with ties broken by run name. Each run opens a pull request against the previous run's branch, the first against the base branch, and nothing is merged.

In both modes, agent bindings must not declare GH_TOKEN; only the Git delivery binding may.

from datetime import UTC, datetime, timedelta

from zeroshot import Client, HostedTarget, StackRequest, StackRun


async def submit_release_stack() -> None:
    request = StackRequest(
        title="Release checkout update",
        repository="the-open-engine/zeroshot",
        branch="main",
        profile="org:software-change",
        delivery="merge",
        expires_at=(datetime.now(UTC) + timedelta(days=1)).isoformat(),
        runs={
            "backend": StackRun(input={"task": "Update the API."}),
            "frontend": StackRun(input={"task": "Update the client."}),
            "integrate": StackRun(
                input={"task": "Verify the combined changes and run the release tests."},
                needs=("backend", "frontend"),
            ),
        },
        submission_key="checkout-release-1",
    )

    async with Client(target=HostedTarget("platform")) as client:
        stack = await client.submit_stack(request)
        status = await stack.wait(wait_timeout=21_600)

    if not status.succeeded:
        raise RuntimeError(f"stack ended as {status.state}")

With a pull-request delivery profile and delivery="stacked_pull_requests", the same runs become the chain backend, frontend, integrate: three pull requests, each targeting the branch of the one before it.

Submission is atomic, and every run receives a stable run ID. needs gates readiness only; stack runs have no output interpolation or shared mutable input. Once its dependencies are delivered, Platform materializes the run against an exact source branch and revision. When materialization completes, readyAt is set and the run's queue deadline is the earlier of stack expiry and seven days after readyAt. With merge delivery, a merge conflict is repaired by the conflicting run itself in the same checkout and delivery loop. A descendant cannot repair a failed predecessor; it ends as dependency_failed. The v1 API has no aggregate event stream, so Stack.watch() polls and yields changed snapshots. Submit a stack covers delivery modes and reviewing a stacked pull-request chain.

docs.title: Pass exact protocol documents
docs.text:
GraphSpec and RuntimePlan wrap exact JSON mappings without loss. Python neither copies the Rust schemas nor applies its own semantic checks:

from collections.abc import Mapping
from typing import Any

from zeroshot import Client, GraphSpec, RunRequest, RuntimePlan


async def submit_exact(
    client: Client,
    graph_document: Mapping[str, Any],
    runtime_document: Mapping[str, Any],
) -> None:
    request = RunRequest(
        title="Repair checkout",
        graph=GraphSpec.from_dict(graph_document),
        initial_input={"ticket": "OE-123"},
        runtime=RuntimePlan.from_dict(runtime_document),
        submission_key="oe-123-attempt-1",
    )

    result = await client.run(request)
    result.raise_for_failure()

An opaque RuntimePlan may carry per-node lanes and passes through unchanged, while UniformRuntime applies one lane to every agent node.

Before starting a local controller or contacting a direct target, the bundled executable performs the same preflight as the CLI.

The Python API reference documents the public client surface.

docs.title: Build a review loop
docs.text:
This guide builds a custom graph that sends one coding task through a worker and two independent reviewers. When either reviewer rejects the change, the loop runs the same worker again with both reviewers' feedback. The run succeeds when both accept, and fails after four passes.

The built-in software-change template already does this with more recovery paths. Build the loop yourself when you want to change the reviewers, their instructions, or the bounds.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
This guide assumes you have completed Run a first task: zeroshot is installed, the Codex CLI is signed in, and you have a folder with an HTTP service to change.

The worker edits the selected folder

Back up work you want to protect, or commit or stash it in a Git checkout.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
The example has three files, plus an optional runtime plan for cross-vendor review. Download them or copy them from the sections below, and keep them outside the folder you are changing, for example in ~/review-loop/, so they stay out of the change.

File Purpose input.json The task review-loop.graph.json Worker, reviewers, loop, and terminal result review-loop.runtime.json Harness, provider, models, and session scopes review-loop.cross-vendor.runtime.json Optional: Codex worker, Claude Code reviewers

The graph controls order and data flow. The runtime plan binds only the three nodes that run agents.

The excerpts in steps 1 to 4 leave out fields; the complete graph is in step 5.

docs.title: 1. Define input and state
docs.text:
A graph starts with a profile, an initial input type, and a policy. The caller supplies only the task:

"initialInput": {
  "kind": "record",
  "fields": {
    "task": { "type": { "kind": "string" }, "required": true }
  }
}

The root seq declares a state record with task plus one feedback field per reviewer, acceptanceFeedback and codeFeedback. The root may add required fields that have an implicit empty value, so both feedback strings start as "" without appearing in input.json.

Every structural node (seq, loop, par, choice) declares its own state type, so the graph repeats this record. Input bindings copy state into an agent's input. Promoted state paths copy updated state from a group back to the group that encloses it.

docs.title: 2. Add the worker
docs.text:
The worker is a step. It reads the task and both feedback fields:

{
  "kind": "step",
  "name": "worker",
  "worker": "builtin.agent.software-worker@1",
  "instructions": "Implement the requested change. If reviewer feedback is present, address both diagnostics before returning. Work in the shared repository and run focused checks.",
  "output": { "kind": "null" },
  "writeBindings": [],
  "attempts": 1
}

The full node also declares an input record and three inputBindings, one per field. Its output is null because the worker changes files in the shared workspace rather than returning data.

The worker value is a label local to this graph. The builtin. names only mirror the built-in template; they add no behavior. Admission derives each worker's contract from the node's declared input, output, signals, and diagnostic, so a label used on several nodes must keep the same declaration and binding kind. Every agent node needs authored instructions.

docs.title: 3. Run two reviewers in parallel
docs.text:
A par group named reviews runs two verifiers against the same workspace. Each verifier returns a verdict signal and a diagnostic, and writes the diagnostic message into its feedback field:

{
  "kind": "verifier",
  "name": "acceptance",
  "worker": "builtin.agent.acceptance-verifier@1",
  "signals": { "verdict": ["accepted", "rejected"] },
  "writeBindings": [
    {
      "value": { "node": "acceptance", "channel": "diagnostic", "path": ["message"] },
      "target": ["acceptanceFeedback"]
    }
  ]
}

The code verifier has the same shape and writes codeFeedback. zeroshot tells verifiers not to edit the material under review; that is an instruction, not a filesystem boundary.

The all join waits for both reviewers. reviews promotes both feedback paths into the iteration state, and the iteration promotes them into the loop state, so the next worker pass can read them.

docs.title: 4. Stop on two acceptances
docs.text:
The loop body is a seq of the worker and reviews. Loops are do-while: until is checked after each pass, so the worker always runs at least once.

"until": {
  "kind": "all",
  "guards": [
    {
      "kind": "in",
      "value": { "name": "acceptance", "source": "signal", "field": "verdict" },
      "labels": ["accepted"]
    },
    {
      "kind": "in",
      "value": { "name": "code", "source": "signal", "field": "verdict" },
      "labels": ["accepted"]
    }
  ]
},
"maxIterations": 4

A loop reports converged or exhausted through its terminated group control. A choice after the loop turns that control into an explicit terminal:

{
  "kind": "choice",
  "name": "loop_result",
  "branches": [
    {
      "when": {
        "kind": "in",
        "value": { "name": "review_loop", "source": "group", "field": "terminated" },
        "labels": ["converged"]
      },
      "node": { "kind": "succeed", "name": "done", "output": { "kind": "null" }, "bindings": [] }
    }
  ],
  "otherwise": {
    "kind": "fail",
    "name": "review_attempts_exhausted",
    "reason": "review_attempts_exhausted"
  }
}

docs.title: 5. The complete graph
6. Bind the agents
docs.text:
The runtime plan has one binding per executable node, keyed by node name: worker, acceptance, and code.

review-loop.runtime.json
{
  "harness": "codex",
  "provider": "openai",
  "size": "medium",
  "nodes": {
    "worker": {
      "kind": "agent",
      "model": "YOUR_MODEL_ID",
      "sessionScope": "node_instance"
    },
    "acceptance": {
      "kind": "agent",
      "model": "YOUR_MODEL_ID",
      "sessionScope": "execution"
    },
    "code": {
      "kind": "agent",
      "model": "YOUR_MODEL_ID",
      "sessionScope": "execution"
    }
  }
}

The worker uses node_instance, so each loop pass continues the same provider conversation. The reviewers use execution, so each review starts a fresh session and does not see the previous pass. The graph state still carries the feedback explicitly either way.

Replace YOUR_MODEL_ID with a model the provider accepts. Nodes can use different models, effort values, or harnesses and providers; size applies to the whole run. The bindings omit connections, so a local Codex run reuses the Codex CLI's login, and a Docker or Platform target derives the canonical OPENAI_API_KEY requirement. See the RuntimePlan reference for every field.

docs.title: 7. Validate, then run
docs.text:
The input supplies only the task:

input.json
{
  "task": "Add a health-check endpoint that returns HTTP 200. Add focused tests and keep the change scoped."
}

From the folder you want to change (or with --cwd FOLDER), check all three files without starting a run. Validation covers JSON shape, graph data flow, loop termination, runtime coverage, and the initial input:

zeroshot run \
  --title "Review loop validation" \
  --graph ~/review-loop/review-loop.graph.json \
  --runtime-config ~/review-loop/review-loop.runtime.json \
  --input ~/review-loop/input.json \
  --validate-only

Successful validation writes {"valid":true}.

Remove --validate-only to start the run:

zeroshot run \
  --title "Health-check endpoint" \
  --graph ~/review-loop/review-loop.graph.json \
  --runtime-config ~/review-loop/review-loop.runtime.json \
  --input ~/review-loop/input.json

Observe and control runs covers status, logs, and stopping.

The same files run on a target with --target platform (see Connect zeroshot Platform) or the name of a direct target. A target requires an exact Git source selected from the checkout or source overrides, and resolves OPENAI_API_KEY from the submission environment or its connection store. The graph has no delivery node, so a target run does not push the accepted change. Add a Git delivery verifier after the loop, or use the software-change template, which defaults to a PR. Choose --push for branch publication or --ship for merge delivery.

docs.title: Cross-vendor review
docs.text:
A reviewer from the worker's model family can share its blind spots. An agent binding can carry its own lane, a harness and provider pair that overrides the plan's default. This runtime plan keeps the worker on Codex and runs both reviewers on Claude Code; the graph does not change:

review-loop.cross-vendor.runtime.json
{
  "harness": "codex",
  "provider": "openai",
  "size": "medium",
  "nodes": {
    "worker": {
      "kind": "agent",
      "model": "YOUR_OPENAI_MODEL_ID",
      "sessionScope": "node_instance"
    },
    "acceptance": {
      "kind": "agent",
      "lane": {
        "harness": "claude",
        "provider": "anthropic"
      },
      "model": "YOUR_ANTHROPIC_MODEL_ID",
      "sessionScope": "execution"
    },
    "code": {
      "kind": "agent",
      "lane": {
        "harness": "claude",
        "provider": "anthropic"
      },
      "model": "YOUR_ANTHROPIC_MODEL_ID",
      "sessionScope": "execution"
    }
  }
}

Replace YOUR_OPENAI_MODEL_ID with a model OpenAI accepts and YOUR_ANTHROPIC_MODEL_ID with one Anthropic accepts. Pass the file to --runtime-config in step 7 in place of review-loop.runtime.json.

A local run needs both the Codex CLI and Claude Code installed and signed in. Before the run starts, zeroshot checks that codex and claude are on PATH; it does not check login state, so a missing Claude Code login fails at the first review. On a target, the run requires both OPENAI_API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and the target must advertise openengine.node-runtime-lanes/v1. The CLI refuses to send the plan to a target that does not.

docs.title: Review a pull request
docs.text: The pr-review template checks a PR's implementation and posts a concise Markdown comment. PR review uses comment delivery so comparison preparation always has an admitted publisher. The --task-from resolver supports GitHub.com; GHE and GitLab comments need caller-supplied graph input. The separate issue-review template retains a basic issue-proposal review; its review workflow will be designed separately. For a deeper static review that reports every verified finding, see Review a PR in depth.

docs.title: What the graph checks
docs.text:
The classifier inspects the captured diff and linked requirements. It requests one reproduction for a fix, feature, UI change, or material correctness, security, persistence, or integration risk. It skips reproduction only for clearly small, uncritical changes such as documentation or a mechanical refactor. Missing tools or services cannot justify skipping a required check.

When requested, the reproducer exercises the changed workflow through the full local stack. UI changes require browser checks. It records command and browser results, including failed checks and environment blockers, without repairing reviewed code. A missing prerequisite remains an explicit verification gap.

The code checker then inspects the diff and its callers for correctness, lean implementation, and clean abstraction boundaries. It checks full coverage of linked issue acceptance criteria unless the PR or caller explicitly declares partial scope, and incorporates the reproduction evidence into the final comment. The comment has a 150-word instruction budget: actionable findings, a brief Reproduction: sentence naming the stack/browser, user action and observed result, and a Setup: sentence reporting startup problems and workarounds, including resolved ones. A skipped reproduction gives its reason. Detailed evidence stays in run history or artifacts. The native header records the captured revisions once.

The native publisher posts the report after these agents settle. A successful run confirms completion and publication; findings or blocked tests can still appear in its report.

docs.title: Prepare the runtime and credentials
docs.text:
The supplied runtime plan assigns all three agents gpt-6.1-sol at xhigh on Codex/OpenAI with independent execution sessions. Save it as runtime.json and pass it through --runtime-config. The publisher is native and has no model. Model choices remain in the caller's runtime plan rather than the graph.

Comment delivery uses the github connection's GH_TOKEN, as other GitHub delivery does. Provide that field through a named connection, the invoking environment, or a native gh login. Publication credentials belong to the native node and are not declared on the review agents.

Local metadata resolution accepts GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, or a native GitHub CLI login. Named targets resolve metadata through their task-resolution route. Hosted targets use host-owned credentials; direct targets need the invoking shell's GH_TOKEN, which the CLI sends only with --forward-gh-token. Targets must advertise task resolution and comment delivery; an older target refuses before submission.

docs.title: Run the review
docs.text:
Select a clean checkout already at the PR head. zeroshot refuses a mismatch instead of switching or resetting the worktree.

zeroshot run --title "Review PR 123" \
  --template pr-review \
  --task-from https://github.com/OWNER/REPOSITORY/pull/123 \
  --runtime-config runtime.json \
  --cwd /path/to/pr-checkout \
  --submission-key review-pr-123

For hosted execution, add --target platform and select a repository environment that prepares the required stack and browser tools. Source comes from URL resolution, so a client checkout is unnecessary. A saved PR review profile already contains its runtime and publisher; use --profile org:pr-review without template or delivery overrides.

--validate-only prepares and validates without executing agents. Ordinary --input FILE passes JSON unchanged and is mutually exclusive with --task-from.

docs.title: Input and result
docs.text:
Fetching happens before the graph starts. PR intake captures {url, context} with title/body, complete context.reviewScope base/head identities, and required context.linkedIssues. Linked issue entries contain {url, title, body} from GitHub's manual or keyword-based closing relationships. Plain mentions do not create that relationship; the checker must report referenced requirements as unverified if their issue text is absent. An empty array means the selected GitHub identity exposed no linked closing issues. Incomplete or erroring metadata refuses preparation; intake never silently truncates issues. The bounded snapshot supports up to 100 linked issues. See GitHub's linking rules.

There is no mandatory task field. Optional caller instructions can narrow review focus or declare partial implementation. PR comparison uses the admitted head against its merge base with the captured base revision, including fork heads; publication refuses a changed review scope. The graph accepts PR context; select issue-review with an issue URL for the separate basic path.

The built-in result retains a receipt; authoritative evidence is in status.metadata.deliveryReceipt, with the comment permalink, identity, and body hash. Comment publication never commits or pushes the review workspace. A custom graph can supply {url, body} directly without an agent or local repository.

Retry uncertain submission with the same explicit submission key and authored configuration. The CLI retains prepared input/source, so retries do not silently read newer discussion text. Resume uses admitted input. One immutable comment belongs to each delivery lineage: matching retries reuse it, while changed report content refuses with its URL. An uncertain POST reconciles remote evidence and fails explicitly if unconfirmed; it never authorizes a blind repost.

docs.title: Prepare a runtime environment
docs.text:
Run submissions to Docker targets accept an environment field alongside runtime:

{
  "environment": {
    "setup": "apt-get update && apt-get install -y jq",
    "startup": "npm ci",
    "variables": { "CI": "true" }
  }
}

Profiles contain graph and agent settings and have no environment reference. Supply the concrete definition when submitting a run. With the CLI, put the contents of environment above into a JSON file and pass --environment FILE alongside your profile. --no-environment sends an explicit empty definition ({}), which bypasses defaults on hosts that provide them. Omitting both flags leaves selection to the host. Direct Docker uses the base environment when none is supplied. Stack manifests also accept a top-level environment; the definition applies to each run in that stack, while omission allows the host to resolve each repository's default.

Hosts may provide saved environments and choose repository defaults before accepting a run. zeroshot executes the resolved definition and preserves it for queued and resumed attempts; it does not store environment resources or interpret repository defaults. The local UI has no environment catalog or selector. Connection values come from the existing target connection mechanism and never belong in scripts or public variables. Only explicitly declared hook connections reach preparation; node connections remain independently declared. If installation needs private registry access, add "connections": { "package-registry": ["NPM_TOKEN"] } to the definition. The CLI can collect hook credentials for a definition you supply. When a host selects a default, its connection store must supply those credentials; the CLI does not inspect saved environments to discover additional secrets in your shell.

docs.title: Example: pinned Node and npm dependencies
docs.text:
For a repository with a committed package-lock.json, save this as setup.sh. It installs OS packages and Node 22.22.3, verifies the archive against the release's SHA-256 checksums, and exposes Node to every agent through $ZEROSHOT_TOOLS/bin:

set -euo pipefail
export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
apt-get update -qq
apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends jq sqlite3 xz-utils

case "$(uname -m)" in
  x86_64) arch=x64 ;;
  aarch64) arch=arm64 ;;
  *) echo 'Unsupported Node architecture' >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac
version=22.22.3
release="node-v$version-linux-$arch"
download=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$download"' EXIT
curl -fsSL "https://nodejs.org/dist/v$version/$release.tar.xz" -o "$download/$release.tar.xz"
curl -fsSL "https://nodejs.org/dist/v$version/SHASUMS256.txt" -o "$download/SHASUMS256.txt"
(cd "$download" && sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHASUMS256.txt)
tar -xJf "$download/$release.tar.xz" -C "$ZEROSHOT_TOOLS"
for tool in node npm npx; do
  ln -sfn "../$release/bin/$tool" "$ZEROSHOT_TOOLS/bin/$tool"
done
node --version

Save the workspace preparation as startup.sh. npm ci rebuilds node_modules from the lockfile, so this also works after restoring a workspace:

set -euo pipefail
test "$(node --version)" = v22.22.3
npm ci --no-audit --no-fund

On your machine, use jq to embed both scripts in a flat environment file, then submit it with your existing profile, task input file, and target:

jq -n --rawfile setup setup.sh --rawfile startup startup.sh \
  '{setup: $setup, startup: $startup, variables: {CI: "true"}}' > environment.json
zeroshot run --profile my-profile --target my-target \
  --environment environment.json --title "Fix the failing test" --input input.json

The file contains setup and startup directly; an inline run API request puts the same object in submission.environment, beside submission.runtime. Setup cannot read repository files because checkout has not happened yet. Startup can invoke a checked-in script, for example bash .zeroshot/startup.sh.

docs.title: Lifecycle and installation conventions
docs.text:
Submission returns after admission and durable acceptance. While the run is admitted, setup runs as root before source checkout or workspace restoration. Startup then runs as the workspace user, with the checkout as its current directory. The graph starts only after both succeed. Watch run logs for phase progress and command output. Nonzero exits become environment_setup_failed or environment_startup_failed; a preparation deadline becomes environment_preparation_timeout. These stop the run without using any graph repair attempts. Force-stop works during preparation and waits for process cleanup before recording its terminal result.

Each hook uses Bash with errexit and pipefail and has fifteen minutes, inside one thirty-minute preparation budget. Install OS packages in setup. Install shared executable tools under $ZEROSHOT_TOOLS/bin, which is on the PATH of every hook and agent, and project dependencies in the workspace. Shell exports affect only that hook; use variables for later commands. The platform's harness Node interpreter remains separate from a project-installed Node version. Setup, startup, and agent sessions have separate home directories; use $ZEROSHOT_TOOLS for tools shared across them.

Workers and reviewers share files, ignored dependencies, generated output, and services. Startup can start a background service; its process belongs to the run and survives individual agent executions. Wait for required services to be ready before startup exits; the runtime does not infer their health. Setup is for installation: start services from startup. Do not daemonize processes or start root services in setup. Setup cancellation cleans up its shell process group; a root script can escape that group, so this is not containment for untrusted root code. The target images suppress Debian package service autostart. Parallel graph branches share mutable state, so scripts and graphs must coordinate concurrent writes.

Both hooks run again on resume: setup, restore workspace files, startup, then restart or continue the graph. Startup must be idempotent with respect to existing workspace files. Checkpoints do not restore running services, Docker images or volumes, database transactions, or agent conversations. A background process may change files while a checkpoint is captured; use application-managed exports for consistent database recovery.

A direct Docker target is an operator-trusted container. Root setup changes that container's OS, including for other runs it hosts. Use separate disposable target containers for independent OS requirements. The target must have a writable root for package installation. Docker commands need an operator-provided daemon endpoint. Detached Docker containers belong to that daemon and are not terminated by the target's process cleanup. Direct target operators or scripts must manage their names, reuse, and removal. When the daemon runs inside a disposable run machine, destroying that machine removes its Docker resources. Local execution uses the invoking machine and rejects setup and startup hooks and their connection references.

docs.title: Submit a stack
docs.text:
A stack is a set of dependent runs submitted to a hosted target at once. It is atomic and immutable: every run uses the same repository, base branch and hosted profile, the target assigns every run ID at submission, and a stack cannot be edited or retried in place. Each run has its own static input, and needs names the runs that must finish first. Dependencies gate when a run may start; they never pass output from one run to another.

The manifest's delivery chooses how the stack lands:

  • merge: each run merges into the base branch before the runs that need it start.
  • stacked_pull_requests: each run opens a pull request against the branch of the run before it, so the stack arrives as a chain of pull requests for review. Nothing is merged.

Stacks run on hosted targets with GitHub.com repositories. There is no local stack execution.

docs.title: Write a manifest
docs.text:
Save the manifest as JSON, for example checkout.stack.json:

{
  "schema": "zeroshot.stack/v1",
  "title": "Checkout update",
  "delivery": "stacked_pull_requests",
  "source": { "repository": "acme/shop", "branch": "main" },
  "profile": "org:software-change",
  "expiresAt": "2026-11-10T00:00:00Z",
  "runs": {
    "api": { "input": { "task": "Add the order total endpoint." } },
    "client": {
      "needs": ["api"],
      "input": { "task": "Show the order total on the checkout page." }
    },
    "docs": {
      "needs": ["api"],
      "input": { "task": "Document the order total endpoint." }
    }
  }
}
Field Meaning schema Always zeroshot.stack/v1 title Stack title; each run is titled <title>: <run name> delivery Required: merge or stacked_pull_requests source The repository (owner/name) and base branch every run uses profile A hosted profile, user:NAME or org:NAME, shared by every run expiresAt RFC 3339 deadline for the whole stack, in the future and at most seven days away runs 1 to 64 runs keyed by name; each has an input matching the profile's graph input and optional needs, which must not form a cycle environment Optional runtime environment applied to every run; omit it to let the host choose each repository's default

The profile decides how each run is built and delivered, so it must match delivery:

  • merge needs a profile with exactly one Git merge delivery node (merge@2 or merge@3), such as the software-change template with merge delivery.
  • stacked_pull_requests needs a profile with exactly one pull-request delivery node (pr@2), such as the software-change template with pull-request delivery.

In both modes, agent bindings must not declare GH_TOKEN; only the Git delivery binding may.

docs.title: Validate, submit and follow a stack
docs.text:
Validate the manifest locally before submitting it. Validation checks the manifest, its deadline and its dependencies without contacting a target:

zeroshot stack validate checkout.stack.json

Submit it to a hosted target you are logged in to. The submission key makes a retried submission return the same stack instead of creating a second one:

zeroshot stack submit checkout.stack.json --target platform --submission-key checkout-1

Submission also checks the profile against delivery and each run's input against the profile's graph, then prints the stack and polls it, printing each changed snapshot as a JSON line until the stack finishes. Ctrl-C or --detach stops following without stopping the stack. Use the printed stackId to follow or stop it later:

zeroshot stack status STACK_ID --target platform
zeroshot stack watch STACK_ID --target platform
zeroshot stack force-stop STACK_ID --target platform

force-stop stops every run that has not finished. Each run in the status has its runId for zeroshot status, zeroshot logs and the other run commands, its needs, and the sourceBranch and sourceRevision it started from once it materializes. A run starts only after every run it needs succeeded; if one fails, the runs that need it end with the error code dependency_failed. Once a run is ready, its queue deadline is the earlier of expiresAt and seven days later. See the CLI reference for every field and flag.

docs.title: Merge delivery
docs.text: With "delivery": "merge", runs follow needs exactly, and a run may need several runs. A run starts from the base branch once everything it needs has merged, so it builds on their changes. Runs that do not depend on each other do not wait for each other. A merge conflict is repaired by the conflicting run itself in its own checkout and delivery loop. The stack succeeds when every run has merged.

docs.title: Stacked pull requests
docs.text:
With "delivery": "stacked_pull_requests", the stack is always one line. When you validate or submit it, zeroshot puts the runs in dependency order, breaking ties by run name, and replaces each run's needs with just the run before it. A run therefore never starts before anything it needed. zeroshot stack validate prints the order. For the manifest above:

{ "valid": true, "order": ["api", "client", "docs"] }

client and docs both need only api, so they are ordered by name, and docs is stacked on client. The first run starts from the base branch and opens a pull request against it. Each later run starts from the branch of the run before it, which its status reports as sourceBranch, and opens its pull request against that branch, so each pull request shows only its own run's changes. A run's work is done when its pull request is open and its required checks pass; zeroshot does not merge it. The stack is complete once every pull request is open.

docs.title: Review and merge the chain
docs.text:
Review and merge the pull requests from the bottom of the stack up. zeroshot and the hosted target never retarget a pull request; GitHub does:

  • When a parent pull request merges and its branch is deleted, GitHub moves the next pull request onto the base branch. Turn on the repository's "Automatically delete head branches" setting, or delete the branch after merging.
  • If the parent was squash-merged, or merged by rebasing, the base branch has new commits rather than the parent's own, so the child pull request still lists the parent's commits. Rebase the child onto the base branch without them, where PARENT_HEAD is the parent pull request's last commit:
git fetch origin
git rebase --onto origin/main PARENT_HEAD CHILD_BRANCH
git push --force-with-lease origin CHILD_BRANCH
  • Changes pushed to a parent pull request during review are not restacked automatically. Rebase each pull request above it onto its updated parent by hand, from the bottom up, for example git rebase origin/PARENT_BRANCH CHILD_BRANCH followed by a force push.

docs.title: Plan a stack
docs.text: The zeroshot-plan skill splits large work into plans whose depends_on lists the plans that must finish first. When plans depend on each other, the skill offers to write a stack manifest to .zeroshot/plans/<id>.stack.json with one run per plan, and leaves delivery for you to choose. See Plan work before running it.

docs.title: Harness adapters
docs.text:
Official local builds include every adapter below. Install each native CLI separately for local use.

Harness ID Providers Distribution codex openai, openrouter, gateway, bedrock, foundry Core claude anthropic, openrouter, gateway, bedrock, foundry Core copilot github, openai, anthropic, openrouter, gateway, bedrock Core pi anthropic, openai, openrouter, gateway, bedrock, github Core opencode openai, anthropic, openrouter, bedrock, gateway, github, opencode, opencode-go Contributed hermes openai, anthropic, openrouter, gateway, github, bedrock Contributed

The claude adapter requires Claude Code 2.1.310 or newer. Before its first model turn it runs the selected executable with --version and fails the node, naming the reported version, when that release is older or the output can't be read.

Local builds enable contributed-harnesses by default. Platform and the default target image disable default features and independently admit only the core registry. Targets advertise enabled pairs through openengine.runtime-harnesses/v1; installing a CLI doesn't enable its adapter.
