Contributed lanes require positive advertisement, while older targets without the extension retain legacy core submissions.

Core adapters receive product maintenance. Contributors maintain their adapters; zeroshot doesn't guarantee contributed-harness compatibility with native releases. Both groups must implement the same full execution, session and Active Memory contracts. Each runtime names its harness, provider and model explicitly. Model identifiers remain provider-owned strings.

Gateway connections carry GATEWAY_BASE_URL and GATEWAY_API_KEY. Pi, Copilot, OpenCode and Hermes also require GATEWAY_API: openai-responses, openai-completions or anthropic-messages. Codex always uses Responses; Claude always uses Messages. Copilot's Bedrock lane uses AWS's OpenAI-compatible Responses endpoint with AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK and AWS_REGION; an optional AWS_BEDROCK_BASE_URL preserves a custom endpoint. Models must support the chosen native API. Codex and Claude foundry lanes share one Microsoft Foundry connection; see Microsoft Foundry.

Local native login works for Codex/OpenAI, Claude/Anthropic, Copilot/GitHub and its OpenAI, Anthropic and OpenRouter BYOK lanes, and Pi/Anthropic, OpenAI and GitHub. OpenCode and Hermes retain native authentication for every supported provider except gateway, including the native AWS credential chain for Bedrock. OpenCode's opencode (Zen) and opencode-go (Go) lanes reuse the native OpenCode account login; a declared OPENCODE_API_KEY serves both. Other lanes require declared connections. GitHub connections use COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN; each harness owns its native exchange and refresh behavior. Declared credentials use private runtime state and preserve saved logins.

Local OpenCode and Hermes runs preserve native configuration discovery with declared credentials. Their declared authentication takes precedence over ambient authentication for the selected lane, while native settings and plugins continue to apply. OpenCode keeps its original HOME/XDG paths and native permission policy. Its declared authentication uses a private plugin, so OPENCODE_PURE=true conflicts with that setup. Native plugins and custom transport code run with the native CLI's authority. Local OpenCode adds no --auto flag and skips configuration inspection because that inspection can start background dependency work.

Hermes uses the interpreter from its installed canonical executable and native configuration factories without attaching to its shared gateway. Local profiles, plugins, MCP and permissions remain native. Declared connections override native dotenv values. Remote backends retain native containment limits. Missing native acknowledgement makes cleanup unconfirmed and fails execution; unreported child usage makes totals incomplete.

docs.title: Execution environment
docs.text:
Every per-node harness child process receives these public, nonsecret execution labels, including agent verifiers and host-owned auxiliary agents. Local and contained launches use the same contract.

Variable Value ZEROSHOT_RUN_ID Owning run's existing ID. ZEROSHOT_NODE_NAME Authored node name, or the auxiliary agent's host-owned name. ZEROSHOT_NODE_KIND Graph kind: step or verifier. ZEROSHOT_NODE_INSTANCE_ID Existing run-scoped node instance; mapped items have distinct identities, while retries and loop revisits retain their instance. ZEROSHOT_EXECUTION_REF Opaque public execution selector shared with logs, attach and diagnostics. ZEROSHOT_NODE_ATTEMPT One-based reducer attempt within the current node visit. ZEROSHOT_NODE_ITERATION One-based iteration of the innermost enclosing authored loop; 0 outside loops.

For outer iteration 3 and inner iteration 2, a node inside the inner loop sees iteration 2. A node in the outer body after the inner loop sees 3. The inner count restarts at 1 on the next outer visit; a node after all loops sees 0. Map indices do not affect iteration values.

Reducer retries keep the iteration and advance the attempt. Fresh loop visits follow the reducer's attempt reset. Harness continuations, provider retries, structured-output corrections and configuration inspection launches retain the dispatch metadata; spawning a process never advances either number. Auxiliary agents use their own run, node and execution identities, iteration 0 outside authored loops, and attempt 1 unless the host request explicitly represents a retry of that visit.

zeroshot applies these labels after environment merges, replacing stale incoming values, with case-insensitive names on Windows. It never changes the controller's process environment or puts labels in credential connections. Descendant tools and hooks may inherit them subject to native harness filtering; remote tool backends retain their own environment policies. Descendants can keep or change inherited labels, so they are not secrets or evidence of authorization. Native control, decision and delivery nodes do not acquire a fabricated harness process.

docs.title: Contribute an adapter
docs.text:
Add an implementation under zeroshot/src/harnesses/adapters/contributed/ and register it in that directory's register function. Core implementations live beside it under adapters/core/; existing public native_v2_codex, native_v2_claude, native_v2_copilot and native_v2_pi module paths remain available to embedders.

A registration supplies a descriptor, provider-access declarations, local path normalization, pure reserved-control validation for harnessConfig, and a factory. Keep descriptors pure: no credential reads, filesystem inspection, process launches or provider requests. The registry validates bounded harness/provider IDs and compatible pairs. Factories receive HarnessBuildContext and return HarnessAdapter with NodeDriver and SessionFactory implementations.

Run closure drains active invocations before calling the optional NodeDriver::close_run hook. Use it to release run-owned bookkeeping while preserving native sessions owned by an ACP session. The hook may be called repeatedly.

Adapters own native protocols, authentication translation and permission handling, including their environment allowlists and home/path expansion. Use shared process and session helpers for private execution files, bounded streaming, cancellation and cleanup. Apply the shared provider_process::apply_execution_environment helper after environment merges for every agent launch. Support workers and verifiers with authoritative response validation, bounded corrections, reusable sessions, live output and usage that reports uncertainty when totals are incomplete.

Install the native Active Memory hook, plugin or bridge in the adapter. Shared memory owns recall budgets, receipts and maintenance; missing acknowledgement means unknown delivery evidence.

Run focused fixtures and shared registry/session tests. The ignored contract in harnesses/live_tests.rs requires a disposable test repository and explicit ZEROSHOT_LIVE_HARNESS, ZEROSHOT_LIVE_PROVIDER, ZEROSHOT_LIVE_MODEL and ZEROSHOT_LIVE_WORKSPACE values. Set ZEROSHOT_LIVE_CLI_BINARY to a separately built CLI's absolute path for memory callbacks. Optional ZEROSHOT_LIVE_CONNECTION_FIELDS lists additional declared field names, separated by commas. Test native bridges too, and check the core-only library:

cargo check --locked --package zeroshot --lib --no-default-features

docs.title: Native configuration ownership
docs.text:
All registered adapters implement per-node native configuration. Keep carrier parsing shared and reserved controls adapter-local. Bind configuration at the invocation or session boundary, never on the lane-wide adapter. Native APIs use object options; CLI arguments remain argument tokens. Preserve the same configuration on corrections, retries and session resumes. Leave unknown native names and values to native initialization. Do not add an option allowlist, portable permission policy, native validation prompt, or generalized inspection subprocess.

Owned authentication, transport, response schemas, identity, memory hooks and containment cannot be replaced through overrides. Existing permission inspection only decides whether to add an automatic local bypass. Native initialization failure must preserve its bounded redacted cause and node/harness identity, settle cleanup, and skip automatic correction/fallback/retry. Focused process/session tests must cover forwarding, isolation, reuse and rejection for every registered adapter.

docs.title: Source-code adapters
docs.text:
Local folders, Git transport, and forge delivery are separate concerns. A local graph without delivery needs no source identity. Contained runs require an exact Git source. The existing push, PR, and merge nodes keep their receipt, repair, cancellation, and recovery behavior across providers.

Operation Required implementation Checkout and push over HTTPS or SSH Shared Git transport Review creation, checks, feedback, and merge Registered forge adapter

GitHub (including Enterprise) and GitLab have maintained delivery adapters. Other Git hosts can use checkout and push; their review and merge APIs need an adapter. See GitHub and GitLab delivery for setup and version requirements.

docs.title: Ownership and registration
docs.text:
zeroshot/src/source_code/provider/ contains effect-free contracts and SourceCodeProviderRegistry. Provider, repository, and review identities are bounded opaque values. Each adapter owns its repository grammar and policy. The shared source identity carries a canonical HTTPS web base, including an optional installation path prefix, separately from the Git locator.

Maintained implementations live in zeroshot/src/source_code/adapters/core/. Contributions live in zeroshot/src/source_code/adapters/contributed/ and register through that folder's register hook. The same registry proves required capabilities during preflight and returns delivery authority during composition. Metadata-only registration must perform no filesystem, process, credential, or network effects. The provider's pure repository_from_remote hook identifies its forge from a credential-free Git locator text after the run boundary validates the URL. Contracts stay independent of protocol and process implementations. The same registry rejects ambiguous matches; both local and named CLI source selection use it. Explicit instance selection uses the same provider's repository_from_remote_at hook; it must prove that the forge repository matches the Git locator. Runtime registration receives the selected source and scoped shared Git transport.

Implement SourceCodeProvider for descriptor and source operations, and SourceDeliveryAuthority for the existing delivery workflow. A forge owns its credential field, repository and review grammar, checks, policy, and authoritative merge result. Git effects reuse the shared transport. A custom API token never acquires GitHub Git authentication authority. Provider credentials are available only through the admitted delivery connection or private source capability.

Adding a forge needs no new delivery node family or closed forge enum. Embedders can register adapters in SourceCodeProviderRegistry and use registry-aware admission. The contribution acceptance test admits an opaque nested repository and review ID, uses its own token field and credential refresh, and drives the existing PR and merge nodes through the supervisor and ledger.

docs.title: Target reconciliation
docs.text:
SourceDeliveryAuthority::reconcile_delivery_target returns SourceTargetIntegration:

  • Integrated { target_revision, outcome }: local reconciliation establishes a concrete target revision and outcome.
  • Deferred: confirmed forge policy owns integration; the adapter establishes no local target revision.

Consumers must handle both variants. Deferral does not advance reviewBaseRevision. Later delivery gates refresh forge policy and require ordinary reconciliation if the forge no longer owns integration.

docs.title: Required behavior
docs.text:
An adapter must observe remote identity before effects, preserve the reviewed candidate SHA and published ancestry, and reconcile confirmed success after a lost response. It must distinguish transport errors, authentication refusal, provider policy/schema errors, and candidate repair. Review creation may allocate a new opaque ID. Merge receipts record the observed integrated revision; requests cannot predict it.

Source credential values stay out of source records, receipts, profiles, and history. Shared transport owns bounded capture, redaction, private SSH files, cancellation, and process cleanup. Recovery preserves the original delivery branch and review identity while obtaining fresh authorized values.

Run the shared provider contract tests and existing delivery tests, plus the contributed adapter's own tests. Include unknown/unsupported capabilities, opaque identities, credential rotation, lost responses, remote branch movement, cancellation, and failed cleanup.

The production registration hook is compiled into the maintained local and hosted factories. An embedder may provide its own registry to admission and use that registry's delivery authority when composing a candidate or allocator. Built-in placements use the contributed registration hook.

The registry's coordinated delivery workflow obtains a scoped adapter through SourceCodeProvider.delivery_authority. Its descriptor advertises the operations that adapter supports. The inspect_operation/operate contract supports atomic operations; maintained adapters return an explicit unavailable error through that interface. Forge credential fields and default connection requirements belong to the registered adapter. Generated delivery bindings remain empty until placement selects the source or comment destination; materialization preserves explicit connection keys and fields. Review receipt links come from the adapter, so consumers never construct a provider's resource paths from opaque IDs.

Conversation comments are a separate operation exposed through the same registry's optional comment authority. Pure URL identification and capability admission do not require a Git source. The native publisher owns bounded create/reconciliation and a durable lineage publication store; the forge supplies actor, comment identity, paginated reads, creation, and exact review-scope checks. Comment authority does not acquire Git transport access or a model session. Its frozen destination includes provider and instance identity. Publication records retain that destination across retries, including GitLab installation prefixes. The adapter validates the exact resource permalink; the publisher also checks actor, body hash, and lineage marker.

docs.title: Documentation versions
docs.text:
Current follows main and is the default. It may describe changes that have not shipped yet. For an installed release, choose its minor version from the header. Each minor version documents its newest published patch: releases 10.2.0 through 10.2.8 share v10.2/, whose content comes from 10.2.8 after that release publishes.

Patch releases update the existing minor documentation without adding another selector entry. Older minor versions remain available.

docs.title: URL contract
docs.text:
The docs base is https://zeroshot.sh/docs/, which serves the GitHub Pages site at https://the-open-engine.github.io/zeroshot/. Resolve these paths against either base:

Relative path Meaning current/ Current main documentation; the site root redirects here vX.Y/ Newest published patch within that minor version versions.json Selector entries: Current and minor versions current/manifest.json, vX.Y/manifest.json Source identity and logical routes dev/ Legacy page redirects to Current stable/ Legacy page redirects to the newest released minor vX.Y.Z/ Previously published patch pages redirect to their minor version

The selector does not list legacy aliases. Existing patch links retain their page, query string, and fragment, but now show the minor version's newest patch. New releases do not create patch paths.

Search engines should index Current. A minor version's page declares the same page in Current as its canonical URL, or its own https://zeroshot.sh/docs/vX.Y/ URL when Current no longer has that page. The publisher reapplies this to every minor version on each publication.

docs.title: Build manifest
docs.text:
Manifest schema 2 distinguishes a docs channel from the exact product used to generate its APIs:

{
  "schemaVersion": 2,
  "docsVersion": "v10.2",
  "productVersion": "10.2.8",
  "pythonSdkVersion": "10.2.8.post1",
  "sourceCommit": "FULL_PRODUCT_SOURCE_COMMIT",
  "publisherCommit": "FULL_PUBLICATION_WORKFLOW_COMMIT",
  "routes": {
    "overview": "",
    "runtimePlan": "concepts/runtimes-and-connections/",
    "runControl": "guides/observe-and-control/",
    "cli": "zeroshot-cli/",
    "pythonApi": "reference/python/",
    "clusterApi": "reference/cluster/api/"
  }
}

The example abbreviates routes; builds list every logical route their source documents, including protocol schemas. Values are relative to the selected version root. Current uses docsVersion: current and null product and Python SDK versions; its source commit identifies main at build time.

A minor's manifest lists only routes its source documents; clients must treat a missing route key as not documented in that version.

Publication tools and this version-policy page can come from a newer workflow commit than the product source. publisherCommit records that distinction. Minor pages migrated from the old site retain their original source identity and omit publisherCommit until rebuilt; their existing rendered product content is reused.

Old patch manifests now contain a schema-2 redirect record such as {"schemaVersion": 2, "redirect": "../v10.2/manifest.json"}. This is JSON metadata, not an HTTP redirect: GitHub Pages cannot redirect JSON clients with its HTML redirect pages. Clients that need an exact historical patch manifest must use the site's Git history. Do not treat a minor manifest as proof that the docs match an older patch exactly.

docs.title: Linking from zeroshot Platform
docs.text:
For a deployed product version X.Y.Z, fetch vX.Y/manifest.json and require schema 2. Confirm that productVersion belongs to the deployed major/minor line, then resolve a logical route against vX.Y/. For example, 10.2.3 uses the v10.2 docs, whose manifest may identify 10.2.8. Callers should label this as minor-version documentation and account for features added after their installed patch. Compare source commits only when the documented and deployed product versions match.

If the minor has no docs, offer an explicitly labelled Current link. Current may contain unreleased behavior. Platform owns instructions for accounts, organization policy, OAuth, GitHub Apps, and capacity; core graph, runtime, CLI, protocol, and SDK material stays here.

docs.title: Publication and recovery
docs.text:
Every main publication updates Current. After Python SDK revision 1, a product release updates its minor documentation from the exact release tag and commit. A retry cannot replace a newer patch with an older one or substitute a different source for the same product version. Later Python-only revisions do not rebuild product docs.

To retry, run Publish versioned documentation. Omit inputs for Current, or supply the exact vX.Y.Z release and source commit for a minor. The optional stable input maintains the legacy released-docs redirect; it never changes the site's Current default.

The publisher consolidates existing patch snapshots before publishing, retaining the newest patch per minor and replacing old pages with redirects. It stages the complete result before pushing gh-pages and deploying through GitHub Pages Actions. No release tags or binary artifacts change. If a release is the first publication, the publisher first builds Current from main in an isolated checkout, then publishes the requested minor from its release source. Both become visible together.

docs.title: Memory lifecycle and storage
docs.text: Active Memory covers configuration, storage and backups.

docs.title: Lesson discovery and maintenance
docs.text:
Workers do not write lessons. After the main graph settles, the built-in postmortem runs inside the same run, using an existing node's model, provider and connections. It has four specialists:

  • Graph maintenance reconciles every supplied graph lesson against its authored node instructions, output contract and procedural operation, including graph lessons qualified by a repository.
  • Repository maintenance reconciles every supplied repository lesson against current authoritative files. Neither maintenance specialist receives or can modify lessons from the other scope.
  • Graph discovery proposes procedural guidance for agent nodes that executed.
  • Repository discovery proposes lessons about recurring work in the repository.

Each maintenance specialist keeps, adapts, retires or defers every lesson in its scope. Large manifests are processed in complete batches bounded by serialized context size; every batch requires exactly one decision per supplied ID. The host binds that ID to its frozen supplied revision and owns revision increments; agents do not manage version counters. Missing delivery evidence makes the specialists abstain. Missing or duplicate decisions fail that specialist's reconciliation instead of reporting success.

Maintenance receives the complete original authored graph and nonsecret runtime, including node instructions, contracts and runtime bindings. Large definitions remain available in complete private files rather than being replaced by truncated prefixes.

For repository-bound lessons, the host records the actual clean checkout commit, when available, in a source: evidence reference. New findings without a verified source basis remain unknown. Adaptation or retirement requires the previous source commit to be an ancestor of the current inspected commit, using local Git objects only, and the checkout must remain unchanged during review. No fetch, authority ref or additional checkout is required. Unknown legacy provenance, dirty or non-Git workspaces, filtered or submodule checkouts, missing commits and divergent or squash histories defer destructive changes; existing lessons remain readable. Such cards need trustworthy revalidation before automatic adaptation or retirement becomes possible.

Maintenance also consolidates overlapping advice within the same repository or exact graph/node/ repository-qualified scope. It keeps or adapts one canonical card and retires redundant paraphrases, while still deciding every supplied ID/revision. Distinct causes and operations remain separate.

There is no findings count quota. Discovery returns every distinct lesson that qualifies; zero new lessons is valid. A lesson needs observed non-obvious learning, a concrete recommendation and a reason to expect reuse. Task summaries, generic advice and facts obvious from nearby code do not qualify. Titles have at most 96 UTF-8 bytes; recommendations have at most 640. The store keeps evidence pointers and provenance separately from the injected card. Use stable paths and identifiers in advice. Admission detects common literal root-relative file:line pointers; semantic maintenance also checks other positional forms. Legacy cards remain readable; maintenance must adapt them to stable guidance or defer, rather than keep or merely renumber their source positions.

Discovery includes observed agent completions and tool receipts without requiring a particular graph shape, failure count, tool count or elapsed duration. Maps, nested loops, retries and partial history do not exclude locally observed evidence. Execution occurrences and attempts keep their identities visible; shared node names alone do not establish causal attribution. The specialist assesses significance, novelty, attribution and expected reuse. A quick discovery or single meaningful failure may justify a lesson; generic advice, waiting time and routine response-format corrections alone do not. Every proposal must cite an observed main-run completion or tool receipt for its actual agent node. Related reviewer evidence may support a worker lesson. Repository discoveries also need a current file citation and a matching file, folder or verified identifier association. Imported history and auxiliary agents never supply fabricated current-run evidence. Maintenance can update supplied lessons independently of discovery. Rejected discovery proposals log the failed validation stage (including card field errors) without logging the proposed lesson text. Postmortem history is read in bounded pages; its fixed transcript budget reclaims old records from the execution consuming the most space, so a verbose late reviewer cannot displace all worker evidence. Reads stop between bounded pages on cancellation. Final context trimming shrinks the largest evidence array first and retains an excerpt per execution where the byte budget allows. Truncation remains explicit.

docs.title: Configuration limits
docs.text:
sourceNode must identify an agent binding in the authored graph. Omit it to inherit the first worker in graph order, then the first agent verifier. All four specialists inherit that node's exact model, effective harness/provider lane, effort and declared connections. They use separate sessions. Each scope's opt-out disables both its maintenance and discovery. A maintenance specialist cannot change the other scope even if its model returns a foreign ID. Only built-in global agents are accepted initially.

nodeInjectionTokens limits graph guidance per node invocation (default 16000), and hookInjectionTokens limits repository recall per native tool callback (default 8000). Each accepts 1 through 64000. These are approximate tokens: one token allows four UTF-8 bytes, including card framing. There is no model-specific tokenizer and no cumulative conversation or run budget. Complete cards that do not fit remain undelivered and eligible for a later matching injection.

budgetBytes is replaced by these two fields; remove it from saved runtime JSON when upgrading.

The postmortem's shared work deadline is timeoutMs, from 1 through 600000, defaulting to ten minutes. Evidence collection, provider startup, investigation, all maintenance batches and conflict retries share that deadline. When it expires, unfinished specialists stop; complete, host-validated specialist results may publish during bounded settlement. A maintenance specialist's decisions publish together only after all its batches finish, preserving related replacements and retirements. Explicit cancellation fences new publication and drains writes already started.

docs.title: Indexing and retrieval
docs.text:
A run freezes an immutable, scoped snapshot. Matching uses resident inverted indexes and performs no model calls, network lookups or filesystem scans. Repository lessons can independently associate with multiple literal files, folders, identifiers or groups of keywords.

Match Score Exact root-relative file 1000 Containing folder 800 Exact whole identifier 700 All terms in an indexed keyword group 500

Each card gets its strongest independent match. Repeated words do not increase its score. Retrieval sorts by descending score, then lesson ID, and returns complete cards within the injection limit. Impact determines admission, so retrieval ranks by relevance alone. An ID/revision is supplied once per provider conversation. Compaction does not reset this deduplication; a new conversation can receive it again.

An identifier is a literal name such as configure_bedrock or CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK. Matching preserves the whole name and also splits snake/camel names into topic words for keyword groups. Groups require two through four specific terms; individual broad words cannot retrieve a card. Matching is deterministic and uses exact terms in this version.

Native path fields take priority. Paths resolve against the tool's working directory and the workspace root, with component-aware folder matching. Shell arguments provide additional signals; simple cd folder && ... commands are recognized. An opaque script that never exposes its file paths can miss relevant cards. The matcher does not trace arbitrary program filesystem access.

Repository cards arrive through native harness hooks:

  • Codex and Claude use PreToolUse additional context through a small native callback helper.
  • Copilot uses its private RPC preToolUse callback.
  • Pi uses a product-owned extension that appends cards to the tool result, including in contained mode where automatic project extensions remain disabled.

Context guides subsequent model decisions. It cannot revise a tool call already issued, so reads and searches provide the most useful early triggers. Managed policy or disabled native hooks can prevent injection. Transport failures leave the task running; missing delivery evidence makes maintenance abstain. Hook receipts record returned context, not proof that the model followed it.

Graph lessons supplement the private provider prompt after admission validation, outside authored instructions. Their scope is the authored compiled graph hash plus node ID, optionally repository. Memory injection never changes that hash, the authored graph, permissions or output contracts. Authored graph changes create a new scope; this version does not transfer guidance across graph versions.

docs.title: Store consistency and run completion
docs.text:
The host owns the database outside the checkout and publishes all shared-store mutations. Workers receive a run-scoped retrieval capability. Reconciliation uses expected revisions, atomic transactions and deletion tombstones, so concurrent runs cannot silently overwrite a newer lesson or recreate a retired record from a stale snapshot. Newly published lessons become available to future runs.

Maintenance can replace lessons or retire obsolete ones. Previous contents are not archived, and there is no built-in undo; deletion tombstones retain IDs and revisions rather than card contents.

The main graph outcome is durably latched before postmortem. Ordinary postmortem failures appear in run logs and preserve that outcome. After a controller restart, confirmed runtime cleanup preserves the latched outcome and marks interrupted auxiliary token usage incomplete. Cancellation stops and drains the optional work; uncertain provider cleanup retains the runtime's existing failure handling. Global-agent work stays outside reducer execution history and checkpoint seeds, while its model usage contributes to run totals.

The native hook records bounded tool receipts in memory for postmortem evidence, including when a tool matches no card. Receipts contain the node, tool name, time and a few associated workspace paths; they exclude arguments and results and do not claim that a tool succeeded. The first and latest receipts survive a fixed 512-record cap. Hidden reasoning is not required or inspected.

Local and target stores do not synchronize automatically. ACP integration is outside this version. Embedders must explicitly select a host-owned memory namespace; the generic hosting configuration does not create an organization-wide store implicitly.

docs.title: History initialization
docs.text:
--ignore-repos and --ignore-graphs accept comma-separated, space-separated or repeated values. Matching is exact and case-sensitive. Repository values match aliases reported in the inventory: checkout folder name, absolute checkout path, admitted repository name, forge owner/repo, or the opaque repo:... namespace. A short folder name excludes every matching repository. Graph values match the exact authored root name or graph hash reported in the inventory; original profile names are not retained in historical admission. There is no --cwd flag.

The first call creates a private session outside repository checkouts and inventories finished local native runs across all repositories. Each run carries its own repository namespace, aliases, workspace, graph name and hash. Checkouts are resolved from recorded workspace metadata, with current remote identity checked against admitted sources. Admissions without a remote are matched against repository IDs independently resolved from the current checkout or its registered remote; folder names and historical display aliases cannot prove identity. A historical remote, when present, still requires its exact remote-derived identity. During inventory, unavailable or changed checkouts are explicit exclusions and do not prevent other repositories from proceeding. Nothing is cloned or fetched. Current checkout probes are shared across runs.

Subsequent calls return the next work through phase and next_action. The skill classifies every candidate, fills the exported specialist response files, and calls the same command to advance. Saved ignore lists apply on resume without repeating flags; conflicting lists require a new session. Discovery findings remain staged until every supplied card has a maintenance decision. The CLI validates the same impact rules and lesson contracts as after-run postmortems; it makes no model calls and uses no provider credentials. Host subagents use the host's model connections.

The newest selected run for each repository supplies its recorded current checkout for maintenance. Graph maintenance covers each exact graph and repository scope; unqualified graph cards shared by several repositories are reconciled once. Repository cards stay within their own repository. Specialist contexts never include another repository's cards. Every selected checkout is fingerprinted, and all mutations across repositories publish in one transaction after complete maintenance coverage. Remote and runtime namespace identities are rechecked before review and publication, including changes to Git configuration that leave tracked files unchanged. If a selected checkout disappears or changes identity after staging, publication stops; restore it or start a new session with appropriate exclusions. Supplied cards are never silently dropped. Citations through symlinks require their canonical targets to be tracked or nonignored too, so the cited bytes participate in the fingerprint.

phase: complete returns the publication receipt. Retrying a completed session returns that result without repeating mutations. Session locks prevent concurrent advancement, including interrupted history export. Atomic SQLite receipts recover a process interruption between publication and its local completion checkpoint; checkpoints use durable atomic file replacement before receipts are removed. Source or lesson changes preserve staged findings for fresh maintenance work; digest-bound task responses prevent stale reuse. Deferred discoveries remain inactive. There is no findings count quota.

Each response retains the source basis exported with its task. A known revision must still match the verified checkout when importing the answer; restore it or start a new session if it changed. Answers exported without a verified basis remain unknown even if the checkout later becomes clean.

Current source includes tracked and nonignored untracked files and executable permissions. Ignored artifacts cannot be maintenance authority. Keep code stable during final review and publication; the filesystem and database cannot share a transaction. The CLI does not pull or change branches. Historical exploration receipts were not persisted, so backfill cannot reconstruct them from elapsed time. Unreadable, unfinished, opted-out and unprovable-repository runs remain explicit exclusions. Old ledgers are read-only; initialization usage belongs to the host session. Platform and Docker target history are outside this workflow.

Inventory can prove an attached run's repository from a unique eligible remote even when its recorded checkout now has detached HEAD. Publication uses that checkout's current runtime namespace, reported per run. Existing local path namespaces do not migrate automatically when a checkout later acquires an admitted remote source.

docs.title: Concurrent maintenance and hosting
docs.text:
Worker recall remains frozen at run startup. Immediately before postmortem, the host reads current scoped lessons and supplies before/current changes separately from the original delivery manifest. Maintenance decisions target current revisions; newly received advice is not evidence of worker use. Publication checks reviewed revisions atomically. A revision conflict refreshes the context and reinvokes maintenance while retaining validated discoveries, within the original cancellation and time budget. A conflict followed by an unchanged visible lesson set stops rather than repeatedly retrying a hidden deletion tombstone. New findings deferred by maintenance remain unpublished. Ordinary transport failures are not revision conflicts.

Storage reads and queued writes stop on cancellation. Backends check the original hard-stop signal and absolute publication deadline immediately before dispatch. MemoryPublicationControl carries both without a forwarded signal. Started writes drain within a bounded storage timeout before cleanup completes.

Embedding hosts may install an authenticated ActiveMemoryBackend through ProductionHostingConfig. Its snapshot and publication operations carry run identity; the backend must derive and enforce the accepted run's tenant, repository and graph scope independently of request fields. SQLite implements the same interface for local and direct-target runs. Hosts must return complete bounded snapshots; failed or partial reads must never masquerade as an empty lesson set.

docs.title: Execution and delivery details
docs.text: How execution works explains graph execution.

docs.title: Process cleanup
docs.text:
When a run closes, zeroshot atomically closes its execution activity; a late process cannot appear after the terminal result.

On Linux, each local command has a private supervisor that also owns descendants which detach with setsid, change process group, or double-fork. It stops and reaps them when the command finishes, the run cancels, or the controller dies. Workspace ownership remains held through cleanup, so a successor cannot resume while that command's descendants can still write. This uses the kernel's subreaper support and procfs; it needs no root access or cgroup setup. Windows uses Job Objects. macOS retains process-group cleanup; descendants that detach can outlive the command there.

docs.title: Auto-research
docs.text:
auto-research runs ten iterations by default. Optional run input options.iterations selects a positive count bound at admission, subject to the engine's general execution and loop budgets. Each normal round has five model executions:

  1. Three independent read-only scouts propose exploration, synthesis, and challenge directions.
  2. One researcher selects the parent and experiment, verifies/restores candidate bytes, runs the experiment, and prepares a supported retained result with compact evidence.
  3. A fresh read-only reviewer accepts the proposed disposition, requests concrete corrections, or approves a justified early stop. A supported non-adoption can be accepted without replacing the incumbent. Plateau alone does not justify stopping before the requested count.

The scouts and researcher keep separate continuing sessions by default; the reviewer starts fresh. Required corrections return to the same researcher without repeating scouting or consuming another research round, then receive fresh review. This work/review cycle has a 64-pass safety limit. Routine file, tool, or archive errors can be repaired by the researcher. Missing optional historical archives and cosmetic bookkeeping issues are advisory when the current result and retained state are supported. Native reviewer outcomes establish approval; no separate file audit counter is required. There are no bootstrap, staging, finalization, or extra audit model passes.

Records live under .zeroshot/research at the shared workspace root, including for tasks in subdirectories. The researcher keeps the charter, current summary, backlog, round evidence, and restorable candidate source there. After two accepted non-adoptions, or diminishing returns across max(1, ceil(iterationLimit / 10)) accepted rounds on one approach, it explicitly reconsiders a new mechanism, an archived parent, and a discriminating measurement. These are reasoned alternatives, not a mandatory parent switch or a fixed gain threshold.

The template supports local results and --push. With --push, the reviewer supplies title and description and one trusted Git delivery node publishes each accepted round. Research agents never use Git. Exhausted review, unrecovered execution errors, delivery errors, and delivery repair requests stop the run explicitly; unreviewed work is never published. Existing saved profiles and admitted runs keep their stored graph and runtime.

docs.title: Delivery feedback
docs.text:
PR and merge delivery consider feedback by default. Use --no-pr-feedback to ignore PR discussion; the git_delivery binding describes the runtime setting.

Automatic repairs accept feedback only from current writers on the target repository. GitHub confirms effective write or admin permission for issue comments, submitted reviews (including unwritten change requests), inline comments and replies. GitLab confirms active Developer-or-higher project membership, including inherited and invited membership, for discussion notes. The account must be active. Enterprise Edition also requires active membership_state; awaiting membership is ignored. Community Edition omits that field, so its response is accepted only after instance metadata confirms the edition. Unknown or malformed membership status fails the feedback read. Permissions are checked again on each inspection and bound to the author's stable numeric identity. Organization association, PR authorship, requested-reviewer status and bot status grant no exception. Confirmed read-only access or nonmembership is ignored and does not start another worker/reviewer round. Failed or incomplete permission lookups stop delivery or use its existing retry handling.

docs.title: Installation and updates
docs.text: Install zeroshot covers setup. This page describes how installation and updates behave.

docs.title: Archive verification
docs.text:
Install the zeroshot command and its agent skills through the npm delivery package, which requires Node.js 18 or newer. The installer selects the release target declared for the current system and checks the downloaded archive against SHA256SUMS before writing the native executable.

npm install --global @the-open-engine-company/zeroshot

docs.title: Update behavior
docs.text:
A canonical CLI release can update its executable and managed agent skills in place. The command selects the newest GitHub release for the current platform, verifies its archive and skill assets against that release's SHA256SUMS, and verifies the new executable before replacing the old one:

zeroshot update

The update does not elevate privileges. Before downloading release assets for a newer version, it checks that the installation directory is writable. A current executable still reports "updated":false when that directory is unwritable; managed skills are refreshed separately. Updates of one installation replace it one at a time. An update that waited for another one and finds the same release already installed reports "updated":false. Before installing a newer release, an update also removes the files that interrupted updates left next to the executable. A download fails with a timeout once the server has sent nothing for 30 seconds; a slow download that keeps receiving data is never cut off. Failures name their cause, such as an unreachable or refusing proxy, an untrusted certificate, or GitHub's explanation of a rate limit. An unwritable installation or rejected archive ends with an npm reinstall command pinned to the release being installed. A release lookup refused with HTTP 403 or 429 instead names npm install --global @the-open-engine-company/zeroshot@latest, because no release version was resolved. The updater uses anonymous GitHub requests. Unchanged managed skill copies are installed or refreshed for Codex, GitHub Copilot, Pi, and Claude Code. A user-edited or conflicting skill is preserved, and the command fails with its exact path after completing any safe updates.

Older updaters install only the skills they know. If zeroshot-graph-design or zeroshot-plan is missing after an executable upgrade, run zeroshot update again. The current updater refreshes all managed skills even when the executable version is already current.

An in-place update of a writable npm installation is supported. It replaces the executables under the package's bin/native directory without changing package.json or npm's installation records. npm list --global therefore reports the npm package version originally installed, while zeroshot --version reports the updated executable. A later npm install uses its selected package version to replace the executables again. To synchronize npm's records with the CLI, reinstall the desired version with npm install --global @the-open-engine-company/zeroshot@X.Y.Z.

docs.title: Managed skills
docs.text:
The package installs the zeroshot, zeroshot-memory-init, zeroshot-graph-design, and zeroshot-plan skills for Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Pi under $HOME/.agents/skills/<name>, and for Claude Code under ${CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR:-$HOME/.claude}/skills/<name>. No agent selection or per-project installation is needed. npm 7 and newer do not run uninstall hooks; after removing the package, remove only unmodified managed skill directories from these locations. With automatic skill installation enabled, CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR must be absolute when set so the global skills have stable locations. Use zeroshot-graph-design for a guided interview to design a graph for your repository.

To install or update only the executables, set ZEROSHOT_SKIP_SKILLS=1:

ZEROSHOT_SKIP_SKILLS=1 npm install --global @the-open-engine-company/zeroshot
ZEROSHOT_SKIP_SKILLS=1 zeroshot update

Only the exact value 1 enables the opt-out. Both commands skip all user-scope skill installation and leave existing skills untouched, even when destinations conflict or are unwritable. Export the variable in your shell configuration to keep future updates from recreating skills you remove. In PowerShell, set $env:ZEROSHOT_SKIP_SKILLS = '1' before running either command. Unset the variable to restore automatic installation and refresh of unchanged managed skills.

docs.title: Windows paths
docs.text: On Windows, the CLI and local in-process runs work natively from PowerShell or Command Prompt. Install Git for Windows and put Git and your chosen harness on PATH; npm-installed .cmd launchers are supported. Local configuration defaults to %LOCALAPPDATA%\zeroshot and run state to %LOCALAPPDATA%\zeroshot\state. ZEROSHOT_CONFIG_DIR and ZEROSHOT_STATE_DIR can override these with absolute paths. The hosted target image requires Linux.

docs.title: Build the workspace UI
docs.text:
Embedding hosts use the workspace bridge contract.

Release executables embed the UI. To build it from source:

npm --prefix ui ci --ignore-scripts
npm --prefix ui run build
cargo build --release --package zeroshot --features ui
./target/release/zeroshot ui

Node.js is needed for this build, not to serve the resulting UI. Library consumers can leave the ui feature disabled.

docs.title: Release assets
docs.text: Each GitHub release includes native archives, the canonical zeroshot-skill.md, zeroshot-memory-init-skill.md, zeroshot-graph-design-skill.md, and zeroshot-plan-skill.md, and SHA256SUMS; archive names contain the release version and target triple.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
The public package is zeroshot; the install distribution is the-open-engine-zeroshot. All I/O methods are asynchronous. Public data objects are frozen dataclasses, and exact protocol documents are copied defensively at their boundary.

The reference is generated from the curated exports in zeroshot.__init__ and their source docstrings:

  • Client and run handle: run and stack submission, lookup, observation, and stop operations.
  • Configuration: targets, run requests, stack DAGs, delivery modes, and runtimes.
  • Result models: immutable run, stack, log, source, and terminal values.
  • Exceptions: request, target, protocol, timeout, and failed-run errors.

See the Python SDK guide for complete submissions and target examples.

docs.title: Version identity
docs.text: The SDK release paired with zeroshot vX.Y.Z is X.Y.Z.post1. This site records that value in its version manifest. If a later SDK-only revision is published, it does not alter an existing core docs snapshot.

docs.title: RuntimePlan
docs.text:
A RuntimePlan says how each executable node in a graph runs. It selects the run size and a default harness and provider, and gives every step and verifier one binding. It contains model identifiers and connection field names, never secret values.

Runtimes and connections explains the concepts, and Build a review loop builds a complete plan for a custom graph. The Rust types in openengine-cluster-protocol are authoritative; the generated protocol schema is the machine-readable contract.

docs.title: Document fields
docs.text:
RuntimePlan is a closed JSON object. The following four fields are required; unknown fields are rejected.

Field Value harness Registered harness of the default lane provider Provider of the default lane, supported by the selected harness size small, medium, or large nodes Object mapping each executable graph node name to a node binding

Optional workspaceCheckpoints is a boolean that defaults to true. Local CLI runs may set it to false to skip workspace snapshot storage and the Restic dependency. Run history, structured outputs, usage, and logs remain durable. Restart uses the retained workspace and original graph input. Selected workspace-checkpoint resume is unavailable when snapshots were disabled. This controls file snapshots, not external side effects or node retry semantics. The current named targets reject opt-out explicitly. The field is accepted in exact and uniform runtime plans and is preserved in saved profiles.

{ "workspaceCheckpoints": false }

Optional activeMemory controls repository and graph recall/collection independently, and globalAgents.postmortem configures the built-in after-run specialists. Both default to enabled on local CLI runs and direct targets. The same sections are accepted by uniform runtime files. See Active Memory for budgets, provider inheritance and opt-out examples.

harness and provider form the default lane. Every agent node runs on it unless its binding carries its own lane. size applies to the whole run. Model, effort, context window, output limit, session scope, and connections are chosen per node.

size is a run-level resource class. zeroshot records it with the run and reports it in run status; the hosting target decides what resources each class receives.

nodes keys are graph node names: 1 to 128 bytes matching [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*.

This plan binds the three agent nodes of the built-in software-change template:

{
  "harness": "claude",
  "provider": "anthropic",
  "size": "medium",
  "nodes": {
    "worker": { "kind": "agent", "model": "PROVIDER_MODEL_ID", "sessionScope": "node_instance" },
    "acceptance": { "kind": "agent", "model": "PROVIDER_MODEL_ID", "effort": "high" },
    "code": { "kind": "agent", "model": "PROVIDER_MODEL_ID", "effort": "high" }
  }
}

docs.title: Harness and provider
docs.text:
Harness and provider identifiers are bounded non-control strings. The host registry validates their compatibility during admission; see Harness adapters for available pairs and where each adapter runs. The same compatibility rules apply to an agent node's lane.

pi/anthropic, pi/openai and pi/github reuse a local Pi login from ~/.pi/agent; the other pi lanes need a connection.

Pi, Copilot, OpenCode and Hermes gateway lanes carry GATEWAY_BASE_URL, GATEWAY_API_KEY, and GATEWAY_API. The last names the wire protocol as openai-responses, openai-completions, or anthropic-messages, so one lane selects the native transport and the model identifier stays opaque and caller-owned. zeroshot never infers the protocol from the identifier, and an unrecognized value fails before launch. Pi's gateway model entry carries a node's contextWindow and maxTokens only when the caller has declared them; omitted limits keep Pi's own defaults. Built-in-provider endpoint overrides keep Pi's catalog and receive no synthesized model entry.

To send Pi's anthropic lane to a caller-owned Messages-compatible endpoint, declare ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL with any one of the lane's credentials (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, or ANTHROPIC_OAUTH_TOKEN); a local run also honors the invoking shell's ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. The endpoint override interpolates the API key only when the connection supplies it, so a token keeps Pi's own environment authentication. Pi's openai lane likewise honors OPENAI_BASE_URL or OPENAI_API_BASE. Pi ignores these variables itself, so zeroshot turns each into a provider override that keeps that provider's own protocol; the openai lane therefore needs a Responses-compatible endpoint, and any other protocol uses pi/gateway. A declared endpoint ends native-login reuse, so the stored login is never sent to that host.

Pi has no permission control of its own, so a contained pi run relies on the disposable capsule rather than a bypass argument.

docs.title: Node bindings
docs.text: kind selects an agent, script, decision, Git delivery, or comment delivery binding. Fields belonging to another kind are rejected.

docs.title: script
docs.text:
A script binding executes a caller-owned program on an existing step, using the step's typed input and output. The step must omit instructions. This initial implementation is local only. Named targets and contained placements reject script bindings.

{ "kind": "script", "command": ["python3", "retrieve.py"], "connections": {} }

command is an executable followed by literal arguments. zeroshot does not invoke a shell. There must be 1 to 128 entries, each at most 8,192 bytes, with no NUL characters and at most 65,536 bytes in total. The executable must be nonblank. Paths resolve from the run workspace. Scripts inherit a small process environment for executable lookup, the user's home directory, temporary files and locale. Public run variables and explicitly declared connection fields are added through the existing connection resolver. Other ambient credentials are not inherited.

The program receives one JSON value on stdin, followed by EOF, and must exit zero with exactly one JSON value on stdout. zeroshot validates that value against the step's output schema. Process input and output are each bounded at 8 MiB. A result must also fit the ledger's 1 MiB serialized completion event, including execution metadata. Complete stderr is retained as bounded diagnostics with resolved connection values redacted. Truncated stderr is omitted because its cut boundary may split a credential. A nonzero exit becomes crash, and invalid or oversized JSON becomes malformed. The ordinary graph error and retry rules apply. Cancellation and the step's optional timeoutMs terminate the process tree through the shared process runner. Linux cleanup also covers detached descendants and controller death; Windows uses Job Objects. macOS process-group cleanup cannot cover descendants that detach themselves. See process ownership. Script steps record zero native model tokens. Services started separately by the application may keep indexes or models warm across script invocations. Service lifecycle is application owned.

docs.title: agent
docs.text:
Field Required Value kind Yes agent lane No Harness and provider; default lane when omitted model Yes Provider-owned model identifier, 1 to 2,048 non-control characters effort No low, medium, high, xhigh, or max; unset when omitted contextWindow No Model context window, 1 to 10,000,000; unset when omitted maxTokens No Model output limit, 1 to 10,000,000; unset when omitted sessionScope No execution (default) or node_instance connections No Connection declarations; empty when omitted

zeroshot passes model and effort to the harness unchanged. It keeps no model catalog and does not check whether a model supports the chosen effort. contextWindow and maxTokens are caller declarations, never inferences: they are validated at admission, emitted only into the pi/gateway model entry, and otherwise left unset for the provider to default. An absent value retains the provider's own limit; a present value must be a positive integer in the stated range.

sessionScope controls provider conversation state. It does not change graph state or bindings.

sessionScope Behavior execution Opens a fresh provider session for each execution of the node, then closes it node_instance Reuses one session when the same node instance runs again, for example across loop iterations

If a reused session is lost, zeroshot fails that execution with session_lost. It does not open a replacement session silently.

docs.title: decision
docs.text:
A decision binding evaluates one categorical question on an existing verifier, using the TypeSafe System One request and response format. It makes a direct HTTP request, with no coding harness or tool access. Upstream nodes must supply the evidence through ordinary input bindings.

{
  "kind": "decision",
  "api": "systemone",
  "model": "jev-1.14.0",
  "minProbability": 0.85,
  "uncertainLabel": "uncertain",
  "connections": {
    "decisions": ["DECISION_ENDPOINT", "DECISION_API_KEY"]
  }
}

All these fields are required. model is an opaque, caller-owned identifier; minProbability is a finite number from 0 to 1, inclusive. The example threshold is illustrative: evaluate it against your chosen model and workload. A decision has no lane, effort, or sessionScope.

The verifier must have instructions, attempts: 1, and exactly one signal. Its signal declares at least two options plus the uncertainty label. For example, route can declare ["simple", "complex", "uncertain"]. Describe each option in the instructions. The adapter sends one Choice question named route, with the remaining signal labels as criteria and null descriptions. The complete bound input becomes state and must be a string, record, or array.

The output must be a record with exactly these required fields:

Field Payload type choice Enum of the options, excluding the uncertainty label probabilities Record with one required number field for each option model string, preserving the identifier returned by the service

The diagnostic must be a record with one required string field named message. The adapter checks the complete distribution, its sum, and its agreement with the chosen option. It emits the chosen label when its probability is at least minProbability; a tie or lower probability emits uncertainLabel. Output preserves the original choice and distribution in both cases. This threshold uses the winning probability, rather than the provider's separate confidence statistic. Use normal graph guards on the signal to select an already authored branch. A decision binding cannot supply the postmortem's agent model. Graphs with no agent bindings skip Active Memory setup; mixed graphs inherit a postmortem model from an agent binding.

Declare exactly DECISION_ENDPOINT and DECISION_API_KEY through named connections. Local runs resolve these fields from the invoking environment; hosted runs use the target's connection resolver. Supply the full POST endpoint, including its path:

Service Example DECISION_ENDPOINT TypeSafe https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone OpenRouter https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone Vercel TypeSafe-compatible API https://ai-gateway.vercel.sh/typesafe/v1/systemone

Use that service's bearer API key and model identifier. The adapter preserves the supplied path and accepts additional response metadata. Endpoints must be absolute HTTP(S) URLs without embedded credentials, a query, or a fragment. It follows no redirects. Requests and responses have a 4 MiB bound and each evaluation has a sixty-second ceiling, within any shorter authored node timeout. Cancellation interrupts HTTP work; a failed request does not silently retry or become an uncertainty signal. Known usage survives invalid answers; unavailable usage remains incomplete. Settled outcomes use ordinary run persistence and checkpoint replay.

The profile editor's Decision model worker creates a verifier with this contract. Choose the model and probability threshold, then bind its evidence inputs and configure the named connection. Changing option labels also requires updating the output enum and probability fields to match. Targets must advertise openengine.decision-models/v1 before the CLI submits or stores a decision-bearing profile. Other question types and provider-specific extensions are outside this binding's current contract.

docs.title: git_delivery
docs.text:
Field Required Value kind Yes git_delivery connections No Connection declarations; empty when omitted pullRequestFeedback No consider (default) or ignore

A git_delivery binding has no model, effort, session scope, or lane. Admission accepts it only on a verifier node whose worker is one of the built-in delivery workers:

Worker Accepts pullRequestFeedback: ignore builtin.git-delivery.push@1 No builtin.git-delivery.pr@1 No builtin.git-delivery.pr@2 Yes builtin.git-delivery.merge@1 No builtin.git-delivery.merge@2 No builtin.git-delivery.merge@3 Yes

The delivery verifier cannot have authored instructions, must use attempts: 1, and must declare the output, signals, and diagnostic of its worker's fixed contract. zeroshot template show software-change --pr prints a delivery node with the current contract.

A graph can contain at most one delivery node, and no other executable node may run in parallel with it, either as a par sibling or inside a map that can have more than one item. A hosting service may require exactly one delivery node; zeroshot Platform quick runs require one. See concurrent workspace changes.

ignore skips pull-request discussion. CI, conflict, freshness, and merge-policy checks still apply.

docs.title: comment_delivery
docs.text:
This binding accepts only kind: "comment_delivery" and optional connections. It has no model, lane, effort, or provider session. It binds a verifier using builtin.comment-delivery.post@1 with that worker's fixed input/output, signal, and diagnostic contracts and no authored instructions.

The node reads a required discussion url and report body, plus optional captured reviewScope. Its URL and present scope bind directly from required caller input; they cannot change before publication. A graph permits one trusted delivery node, and comment publication must follow all other executable work and cleanup, outside loops and maps. The confirmed native result appears in status.metadata.deliveryReceipt, independently of graph-authored terminal output. See Review an issue or pull request.

docs.title: Per-node lanes
docs.text:
A lane is one harness and provider pair. The plan's harness and provider are the default lane for every agent node, and an agent binding can carry its own lane. A node's effective lane is its lane, or the default lane when it has none. size stays run-level.

This plan binds the same three nodes as the first example. worker runs on the default codex/openai lane, and both reviewers run on Claude Code:

{
  "harness": "codex",
  "provider": "openai",
  "size": "medium",
  "nodes": {
    "worker": { "kind": "agent", "model": "PROVIDER_MODEL_ID", "sessionScope": "node_instance" },
    "acceptance": {
      "kind": "agent",
      "lane": { "harness": "claude", "provider": "anthropic" },
      "model": "PROVIDER_MODEL_ID",
      "effort": "high"
    },
    "code": {
      "kind": "agent",
      "lane": { "harness": "claude", "provider": "anthropic" },
      "model": "PROVIDER_MODEL_ID",
      "effort": "high"
    }
  }
}

Each model goes to the provider of its node's effective lane, so here worker needs an OpenAI model identifier and the reviewers need Anthropic ones.

  • lane follows the same harness/provider admission rules as the run level. An invalid pair is rejected when the plan is admitted.
  • A git_delivery or comment_delivery binding cannot carry a lane.
  • A lane equal to the run-level pair is accepted, and the node runs exactly as it would without one. It is still a lane field, so the target support check applies to it and older binaries reject it. Omit lane when a node should use the default lane.

zeroshot starts one harness adapter for each distinct effective lane, and each node runs on its own lane's CLI. Model, effort, session scope, and connections stay per node. Provider access defaults also come from each node's effective lane; see Connections.

docs.title: Target support
docs.text:
Targets that support lanes advertise openengine.node-runtime-lanes/v1 in their discovery document. Before the CLI submits a run or stores a profile on a target, it checks the plan. If any node carries a lane and the target does not advertise the capability, the command fails after reading the target's discovery document and before it requests an access token or sends the plan:

target operation failed: target does not support per-node runtime lanes (openengine.node-runtime-lanes/v1)

Plans without a lane do not require the per-node capability. Targets separately advertise enabled harness/provider pairs through openengine.runtime-harnesses/v1; see Targets. Older zeroshot binaries reject a plan that contains a lane field when they read it.

Local profiles are saved together in one file in the configuration store (ZEROSHOT_CONFIG_DIR). Once any local profile carries a lane, an older binary cannot read that file at all. Every local profile command, --profile local:NAME run, and zeroshot acp session then fails, including for profiles without lanes:

local controller operation failed: local profile store is malformed

To run an older binary beside a newer one, give it its own ZEROSHOT_CONFIG_DIR. To recover, remove the profile or its lane fields with the newer binary.

docs.title: Local runs
docs.text:
Before any agent starts, a local zeroshot run or zeroshot resume checks that each lane's registered executable is on PATH. A missing executable fails the command, and a refused resume starts no successor, with a message such as:

lane claude/anthropic needs the `claude` executable on PATH

A resume that restores a workspace checkpoint checks after the restore, so an executable that only the checkpoint contains is still found. Its message follows controller exited before becoming ready:.

zeroshot acp runs the same check when each session opens, against that session's workspace, and the session request fails with the same message. When every PATH entry is absolute, it also checks at startup. An empty or relative entry resolves against the directory the harness starts in, which is known only per session, so then the startup check is skipped. The check does not inspect login state; a missing login surfaces at that lane's first turn. Lanes with native-login support reuse their harness's login. Other lanes need provider connection fields; see Runtimes and connections.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
nodes contains exactly one binding for every step and verifier in the graph, keyed by the node name. Structural nodes (seq, choice, par, loop, map) and terminal nodes (succeed, fail) never get a binding. Admission rejects:

  • a missing binding for an executable node;
  • a binding for a structural, terminal, or unknown node;
  • a git_delivery binding on a step, or on a verifier that does not use a delivery worker;
  • an agent binding on a node that uses a delivery worker;
  • an agent binding on a node without authored instructions;
  • a worker reference reused on several nodes with a different contract or binding kind.

docs.title: Connections
docs.text:
connections maps a connection key to the exact environment field names the node may receive. Values come from the submission environment or a target connection store at run time.

The example below is the shape a Pi gateway lane uses: GATEWAY_API names its wire protocol and is Pi-specific. Other lanes list only their own provider's fields.

{
  "connections": {
    "gateway": ["GATEWAY_BASE_URL", "GATEWAY_API_KEY", "GATEWAY_API"]
  }
}
Item Limit Connection key 1 to 128 bytes, no control characters Field name [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*, at most 128 bytes Field list At least one name, no duplicates Keys per node At most 64 Field names per node At most 64, and one name cannot appear under two keys in the same node Unique field names per run At most 64 across all nodes

The per-run limit also counts the connection fields and variable names of an attached runtime environment. Each connection value must be 1 byte to 64 KiB with no NUL. The static connection values supplied for one run, counting each key and field name with its value, must fit in 256 KiB.

When a node omits connections, zeroshot derives provider access from that node's effective lane for the execution placement. Local native logins need no declaration; contained targets and non-native providers receive the canonical requirements listed in Runtimes and connections. A run's connection requirements are the union over its nodes, so a plan that mixes lanes can require the fields of several providers.

docs.title: Uniform runtime configuration
docs.text:
--uniform-runtime-config accepts a single agent configuration and expands it into a full plan:

Field Required Value harness Yes As in RuntimePlan provider Yes As in RuntimePlan size No As in RuntimePlan; default medium model Yes As in an agent binding effort No As in an agent binding contextWindow No As in an agent binding maxTokens No As in an agent binding sessionScope No As in an agent binding connections No Applied to every agent node

contextWindow and maxTokens are available in both an exact agent binding and a uniform runtime configuration. They are caller declarations and are never inferred from the model identifier.

Every executable node gets an agent binding with these values, except nodes that use a delivery worker. Those get a git_delivery binding as described below.

When selecting the built-in software-change template, omitted sessionScope defaults to node_instance for worker and execution for its reviewers. The worker retains its session through implementation and every repair; reviewers start fresh each pass. An explicit uniform sessionScope still applies to every agent. Exact runtime plans and saved graphs retain their authored scopes; use node_instance on worker in an exact plan to retain its session. When using the updated template with an older exact runtime config, remove its review_repair and delivery_repair bindings. Existing saved profiles keep their stored graph and bindings.

For auto-research, an omitted uniform sessionScope defaults to node_instance for explorer, synthesizer, challenger, and researcher, and execution for reviewer. The normal round has these five agent bindings; --push adds checkpoint_delivery. Exact plans must supply these node names and their desired scopes. Existing saved profiles keep their stored topology and runtime.

A uniform configuration applies one lane to every agent node. Neither --uniform-runtime-config nor the Python SDK's UniformRuntime can express per-node lanes; use an exact --runtime-config or an opaque RuntimePlan instead.

docs.title: Template delivery bindings
docs.text:
Built-in templates own their delivery nodes. software-change defaults to a pull-request delivery verifier named deliver; --push and --ship select push and merge delivery, and --delivery none omits delivery. The existing worker handles delivery repairs. With auto-research, --push adds only the trusted checkpoint_delivery node; the researcher and reviewer already handle the round records and delivery description. single-worker has no delivery modes.

The CLI inserts a git_delivery binding with no forge connection for push, or {"github": ["GH_TOKEN"]} for PR and merge. Git transport uses the selected source credentials. --no-pr-feedback (requires pull-request or merge delivery) sets pullRequestFeedback to ignore. When feedback is enabled, the forge adapter admits repair requests only from current repository writers, with permissions rechecked on each inspection. See Execution for the GitHub and GitLab authorization rules and lookup failure behavior.

A uniform configuration binds the added agent nodes too. An exact --runtime-config must bind all agent nodes itself. Software-change uses worker, acceptance, and code with every delivery mode. It may omit the delivery node; if it includes it, the binding must be git_delivery. List the executable nodes with zeroshot template show TEMPLATE plus the same delivery flag.

Custom graphs author delivery in both the graph and the plan.

docs.title: Contributed harnesses
docs.text: Official local builds include contributed OpenCode and Hermes adapters; their native CLIs are installed separately. See Harness adapters for available providers, target support and the shared execution and Active Memory contracts.

docs.title: Per-node native harness configuration
docs.text:
An agent binding can include optional, secret-free harnessConfig beside model and effort. It is one JSON object, bounded to 64 KiB of encoded JSON, containing only args (an array of argument strings) and/or options (a JSON object). Each adapter supports the carriers below. Omitting it preserves existing behavior. Nodes sharing a lane can have different configuration:

{
  "harness": "claude",
  "provider": "anthropic",
  "size": "small",
  "nodes": {
    "writer": { "kind": "agent", "model": "your-model" },
    "reviewer": {
      "kind": "agent",
      "model": "your-model",
      "harnessConfig": { "args": ["--tools", "Read,Grep,Glob"] }
    }
  }
}
Harness Carriers Example harnessConfig Codex args for native exec/exec resume options {"args":["--config","web_search=\"disabled\""]} Claude Code args for native print mode; one inline --settings JSON object is supported {"args":["--tools","Read,Grep,Glob"]} Copilot options for native session.create / session.resume parameters {"options":{"availableTools":["view","grep"]}} Pi args for native JSON mode {"args":["--tools","read,grep"]} OpenCode args for native run; options for native inline configuration {"options":{"permission":{"edit":"deny"}}} Hermes options over its native loaded configuration before native policy/agent construction {"options":{"agent":{"max_turns":12}}}

Argument strings are passed directly, without a shell. Native options retain native semantics: unknown JSON keys may be accepted or ignored, and native versions may behave differently. zeroshot validates the envelope and reserved controls, not a catalog of native settings or tools. This feature does not guarantee a read-only filesystem or protect tests/ when an allowed native tool can write files.

args configures native options; positional task messages and unbound @file inputs are reserved for zeroshot. Each CLI adapter recognizes its native separated option operands (including Claude's variadic tool lists and Pi's --tools -read). For other option syntax, bind a value explicitly with the harness's joined form, such as --native-option=value; unknown option names still reach the harness. Native values are not validated or translated. A bare value after a no-value switch is rejected with its harnessConfig.args index instead of being appended or queued as another prompt.

Overrides apply only to that node's invocation/session and remain present on correction turns, provider continuation, and node-instance revisits. Native configuration discovery remains enabled as before; supplied values override only supported settings. OpenCode/Hermes objects merge recursively with existing native objects; supplied arrays/scalars replace their native values. User and repository configuration files are never edited. Changing a lane preserves the authored object for review; the new harness interprets it without translation. JSON import/export and saved profiles retain it. Python RuntimePlan mappings accept it unchanged; UniformRuntime(harness_config=...) supplies the same object to every generated agent binding.

zeroshot reserves model/provider selection and credentials, private state, workspace/session identity, transport, prompt and response contracts, required hooks, and cleanup/cancellation. Conflicts identify the node, harness and configuration path or flag. Credentials must use declared connections. Opaque Claude --settings files and runtime-changing Codex profiles are excluded because they can replace owned controls; ordinary native user/project discovery still works. Contained placements also retain host-owned permission/resource requirements. Locally, nonempty Claude/Codex overrides suppress automatic permission bypass; permission inspection never becomes arbitrary CLI validation.

Hook-trust bypass and session redirection are reserved, including Codex --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust and --worktree, Claude --safe-mode, --background/--bg and --cloud, and Pi --fork. Contained Pi also owns tool selection and project trust under their native aliases, including -t/--tools and -a/--approve. Local Pi tool modifiers such as {"args":["--tools","-read"]} are passed through: Pi's exact short tokens do not treat -read as the reserved -r option. OpenCode --pure (including joined forms) is reserved because it disables the runtime's authentication and Active Memory plugins.

Codex exec subcommand tokens (resume, fork, review, help) are runtime-owned anywhere in args; if a native option needs one as a literal value, use its --option=value form. Codex prompt attachments (--image/-i) are also runtime-owned. Claude reserves --from-pr, --teleport, --system-prompt-file and --append-system-prompt-file to preserve session and prompt ownership.

Generated review-loop reviewers and built-in auxiliary memory agents retain inherited harnessConfig, so copying a binding does not broaden its native restrictions. Reviewers still receive fresh sessions and do not inherit credentials. Built-in defaults are unchanged when configuration is absent. Active Memory installs its existing hooks/plugins independently; Claude inline settings compose with its owned hook in a single layer. Restrictions can prevent an auxiliary agent from completing its work.

A native launch or session-initialization rejection fails the node with the native cause through normal bounded, redacted diagnostics and authored error routing. It does not trigger response correction, configuration fallback, or adapter retries of rejected initialization. Settings accepted or ignored by the native harness have no effective-configuration acknowledgement or added preflight.

docs.title: Target runtime contracts
docs.text: Targets covers choosing and connecting a target.

docs.title: Discovery and sizes
docs.text:
Targets advertise their enabled harness/provider pairs through the openengine.runtime-harnesses/v1 discovery extension. The CLI checks every selected lane before requesting an access token or submitting a run or profile, and the target enforces its catalog again during admission. Older targets without this extension accept only the established core harnesses through client preflight.
